+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text. *OXYGEN PARTIAL PRESSURE: 160 MM HG.* *CABIN GRAVITY: 0.38 G (SIMULATED).* *BEARING: HIGH MARS ORBIT, VECTOR 9-SUB-FOUR.* Arthur Neegan stared at the phosphor characters until they blurred into emerald smears against the dull grey alloy of the bulkhead. He rubbed his knuckles, the skin still embedded with the fine, reddish ochre of the Lacus Soli basin. Three hours ago, he had been drinking chicory tea at his survey desk, listening to the monotonous thump of the atmospheric scrubbers. Then had come the chime at the airlock, followed by four men in tailored vacuum-drill suits bearing the double-crescent crest of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Diplomats did not carry sidearms calibrated for sub-dermal disruption, nor did they possess personal transport skiffs capable of pulling three gravities out of the gravity well without burning out their coils. The hatch hissed open with a hydraulic shudder. An orderly with rigid posture and a collar buttoned to the throat bowed stiffly. "Mr. Neegan. The Plenipotentiary will receive you." Arthur stood, adjusting the collar of his utility tunic. He felt woefully out of place, a creature of soil core-samplers and seismic thumper-rigs suddenly translated into a world of polished beryllium and soft-shod footfalls. He stepped out of the holding cubicle into a wide corridor that smelled faintly of dry ozone and expensive tobacco. The ship, he realized as they passed an observation port, was not merely an orbital cutter. Hanging against the curved, rust-streaked marble of Mars was the long, dagger-like silhouette of an Antares-class dreadnought, its radiator vanes glowing dull cherry-red against the void. He was ushered into an octagonal saloon. One entire wall was composed of polarized quartz, framing the sunlit crescent of the red planet below. Standing before it, swirling an amber liquid in a crystal tumbler, was a slender man with silver hair clipped close to his skull. He wore a severe tunic of midnight blue, entirely unadorned except for a modest platinum bar at the breast. "You have been calculating the odds, Mr. Neegan," the man said without turning around. His voice had the dry, clipped cadence of the Inner Ring academies. "A miner’s habit, I believe. Calculating the yield per ton, the cost of drill bits, the probability of cave-in." "I calculate that your men owe me for a broken hydraulic seal on my outer lock," Arthur said flatly. "And that kidnapping an independent leaseholder violates Article Seven of the Martian Charter." The man turned, a thin smile touching his lips. "The Charter was drafted by the United Earth Mining Syndicate when Mars was considered an iron desert populated by malcontents and bankrupt geologists. That was sixty years ago. Before you brought up a core sample from Sector Twelve that registered seventy-four on the Becquerel-Vance catalytic scale." He gestured toward a low armchair upholstered in synthetic seal-leather. Arthur remained standing. "I am Minister Theron," the man continued, unbothered. "Of the Antares Council of Trade and Security. Please, sit. We are men of practical science, Arthur. Let us dispense with the theatrical indignation." "If you're practical," Arthur said, "you know that Azra isn't just another heavy metal. It isn’t pitchblende. You don't refine it; it refines everything around it. My instruments didn't just register catalytic decay—they nearly melted because the ambient thorium in the bedrock began shedding half-lives like water through a sieve." "Precisely," Theron said softly. He stepped forward, setting his glass upon a desk of polished Martian basalt. "Under normal conditions, a standard hyper-spatial coil requires fifty metric tons of enriched californium to punch through the Einstein-Minkowski boundary. The mass ratio makes interstellar commerce sluggish, centralized—and entirely dependent on Earth’s monopoly of the oceanic heavy-water beds. But three kilograms of Azra, acting as a sub-atomic accelerator? It reduces that mass requirement by a factor of ten thousand." Theron leaned in, his eyes bright with an intellectual hunger that Arthur recognized instantly. It was the same madness that drove men into the desolate red canyons with nothing but a pick and an oxygen candle. "Azra is not merely fuel, Arthur. It is the end of distance. It is also, regrettably, the means by which a single defensive torpedo can induce spontaneous fission in the core of an enemy dreadnought before it clears low orbit. Do you understand the stakes now?" "I understood them the moment my counters went off the scale," Arthur replied, his voice cold. "And I understand that Earth’s Combine ships are already decelerating from the Jovian perimeter. You didn't invite me here to discuss nuclear physics, Minister. You brought me here because my claim is filed in the public registry at Bradbury City, and under corporate law, you cannot mine a square centimeter of Sector Twelve without my physical signature on the transfer deed." Theron laughed—a short, genuine bark of amusement. "You first-generation pioneers are delightfully stubborn. Yes, the legalities matter. Even in the shadow of war, the illusion of contract must be maintained. The Earth Combine considers Mars a penal colony with an atmosphere problem. They will offer you a standard indemnity—perhaps twenty thousand credits—and a sudden, fatal depressurization accident in your bunk three weeks later." Theron walked to the desk, pressing a stud. A miniature holographic emitter flickered to life, projecting a glowing document above the stone surface. "Antares offers you something different," Theron said, his tone dropping into an intimate, seductive rhythm. "One billion credits, deposited in the neutral banks of Ganymede. A hereditary seat on the colonial advisory board. And, most importantly, immediate transit for you and your family to the outer systems, aboard this vessel, before the Earth blockade closes the Martian shipping lanes permanently." Arthur looked at the glowing blue letters hovering in the air. The sum was staggering, enough to buy an entire fleet of ore-freighters. It was wealth beyond the dreams of any dirt-scratcher on the frontier. "And if I refuse?" Arthur asked. Theron picked up his tumbler again, gazing down at the red sphere beneath them. "You are an engineer, Neegan. You know what happens when a system is subjected to pressure it was never designed to hold. Earth will not permit us to hold the Azra vein. We will not permit them to seize it. Mars will become the anvil upon which two galactic empires hammer out their supremacy." Theron turned back to Arthur, the smile gone, replaced by a terrible, sober clarity. "Sign the deed, Arthur. Let us hold the vein, and we will protect this world. Refuse, and your unassuming plot of sand will be the crater in which civilization burns." Arthur looked from the document to the cold, black vacuum outside the quartz window. In the distance, among the fixed constellations, a tiny spark of light flickered: the drive-flare of an incoming Earth cruiser. The clock had already run out.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens effectively with Arthur aboard the vessel, per the prompt, and delivers a dialogue-heavy confrontation with a mysterious minister, an offer, and hints of larger intrigue (Earth Combine vs. Antares, blockade threats, weaponization of Azra). The Asimovian flavor is present: dialogue-driven exposition of scientific/political concepts, a rational protagonist, big-picture economics of interstellar travel, and a chess-like negotiation. The retrofuturistic details (phosphor screens, chicory tea, holographic emitter) work well. Strengths: The dialogue is crisp and functional, with Arthur's legal claim as leverage being a clever, Asimov-like touch. The stakes are clearly articulated. The prose is clean and controlled, with vivid but economical imagery (dreadnought's radiator vanes glowing cherry-red, ochre embedded in knuckles). Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat formulaic — the suave villain-minister offering a deal is a stock scene, and Theron is a fairly thin character. The exposition is heavy-handed at times (Theron's physics lecture reads as info-dump). The ending's incoming Earth cruiser is a convenient dramatic beat. Arthur's characterization is competent but not deeply nuanced; his stubbornness is asserted more than revealed. Still, the piece is coherent, well-paced, and faithful to the prompt's requirements. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 78.7
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The safelight turned the darkroom into a wound: deep, amber-red, and thick with the sour vinegar bite of stop bath. In normal light, I knew exactly who I was. I was twenty-five, the girl with the blunt-cut bangs, the vintage motorcycle boots, and the reputation for steering every conversation, critique, and romantic encounter with a steady, unapologetic hand. I liked my men like I liked my prints: high contrast, sharp-edged, neatly categorized. Then came Elliot. He stood beside me at the developing tray, his silhouette bathed in crimson. Nineteen, with cheekbones that could cut glass and a wardrobe that looked like the Cure had collided with an estate sale—torn fishnets under a shredded mohair cardigan, battered creepers, and silver rings stacked to his knuckles. Yet there was nothing sharp about his presence. He was quiet water. Elliot gripped the bamboo tongs, gently agitating the plastic tray. Slosh. Slosh. Beneath the rhythmic wash of the developer, he began to hum—a faint, melancholic melody, something post-punk slowed down to a lullaby. It vibrated softly against the low hum of the exhaust fan. "You always hum when you're anxious," I said, leaning my hip against the dry bench, keeping my voice deliberately casual. His humming hitched. He didn't look up, but the red light caught the faint curve of a blush high on his cheeks. "I didn't realize I was doing it out loud." "It’s not bad," I said, softening the edge before it could nick him. "It’s nice. What are we pulling?" "Just... the portraits from Tuesday. The self-portraits." His hands were trembling slightly. Normally, my instinct in moments of hesitation was to take over. I’d reach out, cover their hands with mine, steer the wheel. In relationships, I was the architect. I gave directions, set the pace, took what I wanted with a grin that dared anyone to object. But with Elliot, that impulse felt heavy-handed, almost violent. He wasn't someone to be conquered; he was someone who needed room to exist without being crowded out. He tipped the tongs, lifting an eight-by-ten sheet from the bath. As the liquid sheeted off the paper, an image resolved through the murk. It was Elliot, but stripped of his usual heavy eyeliner and dark wool. He was wearing an ivory slip dress, silk clinging to his slight frame, his gaze averted from the camera, one hand resting delicately on his collarbone. The lighting was chiaroscuro, tender and devastatingly intimate. My breath caught in my throat. "Elliot." "I almost didn't print it," he whispered, staring down at his own likeness. He set the print into the stop bath. "I’ve been... trying to figure out how to say it out loud. Or even if I have to say it." I stayed completely still. My heart hammered against my ribs, a strange mix of fierce, protective heat and something else—something raw and illicitly electric. "Say what?" I asked gently. He swallowed. I watched the movement of his throat. "I don't think I'm just playing dress-up anymore, Dani. I don't know if 'boy' is... the whole truth. Or if it's the truth at all." He paused, his knuckles whitening on the edge of the sink. "Sometimes I look in the mirror and the masculinity I perform feels like a jacket that’s three sizes too tight in the shoulders. But when I took that photo... I felt like I was actually in the room. Not just haunting it." The red darkness seemed to close in around us, warm and womb-like. A confessional booth without the priest. My mind spun, struggling to recalibrate. For years, my attraction had been an open-and-shut case: I liked men. I liked the friction of traditional masculinity pushing against my own dominant energy. But looking at Elliot right now, hearing the raw, fragile honesty trembling in his voice, my desire didn't waver. It flared. It wasn't despite his ambiguity; it was *because* of it. There was a breathtaking courage in the way he was unspooling himself right in front of me. To stand in the liminal space, undefined, searching—it was the most magnetic thing I’d ever witnessed. And it terrified me. What did it say about me, the woman who took pride in knowing every angle of her own desires, that I was falling hard for someone whose edges were dissolving before my eyes? "Does it scare you?" Elliot asked. He turned to me fully then, his dark eyes enormous under the safelight, searching my face for disgust, for mockery, for pity. I hated that he expected any of those things. My hands twitched in my pockets. I wanted to pull him against me, bury my face in the crook of his neck, and tell him I’d break the jaw of anyone who made him feel small. But that was my ego talking—my need to be the hero, the protector, the one in control. He didn't need a bodyguard. He needed a witness. I took half a step forward, closing the distance between us until the scent of his clove cigarettes and dusty wool filled my lungs. I kept my hands at my sides, deliberately giving him the choice to step back. He didn't. "No," I said, my voice lower than usual, thick with an honesty that felt unfamiliar in my own mouth. "It doesn't scare me, Elliot. It’s gorgeous. You’re gorgeous." His breath hitched. "Even if... even if I don't know where I'm landing yet?" "I don't care about the landing," I murmured, leaning in just an inch more, letting the heat of my skin radiate against his. "The flight looks incredible on you." A breath of a laugh escaped him, half a sob, and the tension in his narrow shoulders broke. Slowly, with an agonizing tentativeness that made my stomach swoop, Elliot reached out. His cool, chemically scented fingertips brushed against the bare skin of my wrist, testing the waters. I didn't seize his hand. I didn't pull him in for the fierce, breathless kiss my body was screaming for. Instead, I simply turned my palm upward, letting him lace his fingers through mine on his own terms. He smiled, shy and luminous, and for a moment, the darkroom felt like the only room left on earth. "We need to move the print to the fixer," he whispered, not letting go of my hand. "Yeah," I said, my pulse fluttering against his thumb, entirely undone by this boy—or whoever he was becoming—and thrilling at the fact that for once in my life, I had no idea what was going to happen next. "Let’s see what else comes into focus."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a strong execution of a demanding prompt. The darkroom setting is used effectively—the red safelight, developing chemicals, and the self-portrait print serve as both atmosphere and plot device, with the reveal of Elliot's slip-dress portrait functioning as the narrative's visual confession. Dani's voice is consistent: assertive, wry, image-conscious, and her internal conflict between control and restraint is well dramatized through concrete choices (not seizing his hand, turning her palm up). The dialogue is mostly natural, with a few lines tipping toward the aphoristic ("The flight looks incredible on you" is a bit slick for the moment, though it lands as characterful bravado). Elliot's dialogue is tender and believable, with the "jacket three sizes too tight" metaphor feeling earned and specific. Weaknesses: some metaphors strain ("the darkroom into a wound," "quiet water," "confessional booth without the priest"—the last is decent but the accumulation edges toward overwrought). The prose occasionally over-polishes, stacking sensory details for effect rather than necessity. The resolution is somewhat quick and smooth—Elliot's fear dissolves fast, and the ending is warm, though the prompt explicitly requested tender awkwardness and emerging chemistry, so the positivity is largely congruent with the brief rather than incongruent. The transformation of both characters is seeded well (Dani's established pattern of dominance, Elliot's established anxiety), so nothing feels unearned. The piece is coherent, emotionally layered, and engaging throughout, though it plays within conventions of the "confessional intimacy" genre without much risk-taking at the structural level. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 77.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### I. The Trevi Skid The smell of burnt rubber overtook the faint, mineral mist of the Trevi Fountain. Ben had been trying to reconcile a dense paragraph on Nicola Salvi’s travertine façade with the sheer, churning mass of tourists when the roar of a single-cylinder engine sheared through his thoughts. He stepped backward off the curb; a horn blared like an angry hornet, and a battered red Moto Guzzi skidded sideways across the basalt cobblestones, stopping precisely two inches from his knee. Ben dropped his *Blue Guide*. "Good heavens—*mi scusi*, I am so profoundly—" The rider kicked the stand down and yanked off a matte-black helmet. A cascade of dark, sweat-damp curls spilled out, framing high cheekbones, flashing amber eyes, and a mouth drawn into a furious, sharp line. "Are you completely blind, or do you just worship the pavement?" she fired in rapid Romanesco, her voice a gravelly melody. "You cross like a pigeon with a death wish!" Ben blinked, clutching his tweed jacket to his chest like a shield. "I… *parla inglese?* I was reading about the aqueduct." She stared at him, taking in the rumpled linen, the wire-rimmed glasses askew on his nose, and the crimson flush crawling up his neck. Her glare cracked. A sudden, dangerous amusement danced in her eyes. "An Englishman," she sighed, switching to accented, razor-sharp English. "Of course. Studying history while trying to become it. I am Alessandra." "Ben," he stammered, bending awkwardly to retrieve his scuffed book. "Benjamin. I really am sorry." Alessandra tapped the spare helmet strapped to the pillion seat. "Apology rejected unless you let me fix your education, Professore. You’ve been looking at the stone. You haven’t seen the city." "I have an itinerary—" "Burn it," she said, tossing him the helmet. "Get on." *** ### II. Via dei Coronari Holding onto Alessandra was a terrifying, sensory assault. She smelled of unburned petrol, sea-salt spray, and bitter orange blossom. Rome blurred past them in flashes of ochre plaster, fluttering laundry, and the startled shouts of taxi drivers as she threaded the narrow alleys like a needle. They stopped at a tiny, standing-room-only bar tucked into an alley off Via dei Coronari. Alessandra ordered two *cremine* without asking. "Drink it fast," she commanded, leaning her elbows against the zinc counter. "Before the heart stops racing." Ben obeyed, the velvety, sugar-whipped espresso burning his tongue. "Do you drive like that for your deliveries, or just when you’re hunting pedants?" "Both," she grinned. Her hand lingered near a brass sugar bowl shaped like a sleeping cat. With a flick of her wrist so casual it seemed like an optical illusion, the cat vanished into the deep pocket of her leather jacket. Ben choked slightly on his coffee. His eyes widened. "Did you… did you just—?" "Just what, Benjamin?" Her gaze was wide, entirely innocent, and completely dared him to say it aloud. "Nothing," he managed, his pulse thumping erratically against his collar. A strange, illicit jolt of electricity hummed beneath his sternum. "Nothing at all." "Good boy," she murmured, wiping a drop of foam from the corner of his lip with her thumb. Her skin was warm, calloused from the throttle. "Now come. The light is changing." *** ### III. The Ghetto In the quiet shade of the Jewish Ghetto, beneath the towering arches of the Portico d’Ottavia, a broad-shouldered man unloading crates of artichokes looked up and dropped his clipboard. "Ale?" the man called out, wiping his hands on an apron. "Ale, *dio mio*, you’re still alive?" Alessandra stiffened slightly, then plastered on a dazzling, theatrical smile. "Enzo! Still selling weeds to tourists?" They exchanged rapid, theatrical kisses on both cheeks. Enzo’s dark eyes shifted immediately to Ben, taking in the academic’s hopelessly proper posture and disheveled hair. "Who’s the stray?" Enzo asked in Italian, then turned directly to Ben, his tone dropping into dry, cautionary English. "Listen to me, my friend. Whatever she told you she does, double the speed and halve the truth." "Enzo, shut up," Alessandra said, rolling her eyes. "I’m serious, mister," Enzo continued, leaning toward Ben with a conspiratorial squint. "She’s got quick hands and zero conscience. Last summer she walked out of my cousin’s wedding with the centerpiece and his vintage Vespa keys. Check your pockets every ten minutes. If she smiles at you like that, she’s already stolen your watch." Alessandra smacked Enzo’s chest with the back of her hand, laughing, but there was a flicker of genuine heat in her cheeks. "He’s a scholar, Enzo. He doesn't have anything worth taking." "Is that a challenge?" Ben heard himself say. The words slipped out before his internal censor could stop them. Both Alessandra and Enzo turned to look at him. Alessandra’s lips parted, her eyebrows arching with genuine surprise—and an unmistakable, predatory delight. "See?" Enzo muttered, backing away with his hands raised. "Already poisoned. Good luck, Professore." *** ### IV. The Gianicolo Overlook Dusk settled over the city like crushed velvet, turning the Tiber into a ribbon of molten bronze. They stood at the balustrade of the Janiculum Hill, the entirety of Rome spread beneath them in a tapestry of illuminated domes and ancient tile. Ben leaned against the cold stone, exhausted, disoriented, and entirely alive in a way he hadn't felt in a decade. "I should be angry with you," he said softly. "You dragged me across four neighborhoods, broke roughly thirty traffic laws, and I’m ninety percent sure you stole a decorative salt cellar from that trattoria in Trastevere." "Seventy percent," she corrected, resting her hip against his. "And you didn't run away." "I couldn't catch my breath long enough to run." Alessandra turned to face him, the ambient glow of the streetlamps catching the gold flecks in her eyes. The mocking, whirlwind facade softened, leaving something raw and unexpectedly quiet in the space between them. "You spend your life reading about what men built two thousand years ago," she murmured, stepping closer, until the leather of her jacket brushed his lapels. "Don't you want to live in what’s happening now?" Ben looked down at her. His hand, entirely of its own accord, reached out and tucked a stray, windblown curl behind her ear. "I think I might be terrified of what’s happening now." "Good," she whispered. She leaned up on her toes and kissed him. It was neither hesitant nor polite; it tasted of strong coffee, cold evening air, and pure, reckless momentum. Ben’s hands gripped her waist, pulling her flush against him, surrendering his careful, quiet world to the Roman night. When she finally pulled back, her breath came shallow and fast. A triumphant, enigmatic smirk tugged at the corners of her mouth. She reached into her jacket, pulled out an object, and dropped it into his palm. It was his grandfather’s gold wristwatch, which had been strapped securely to his wrist when he woke up that morning. "Tomorrow morning," Alessandra said, stepping toward her motorcycle, eyes glittering in the dark. "Eight sharp. Piazza Navona. Don't be late, Benjamin. I have your time."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a polished, well-structured romance vignette that fulfills the prompt with confidence. The scene structure (four numbered sections across one day) gives it momentum, and the Trevi near-miss opening efficiently establishes both characters. Alessandra's kleptomania is handled well: shown through the sugar-bowl lift, the salt cellar, and the final watch reveal rather than stated outright — a strong "show" choice. Enzo functions as an effective third-party mirror, warning Ben and thereby raising stakes and characterizing Alessandra through another's eyes. Strengths: crisp, witty dialogue with distinct voices (Romanesco sharpness vs. Ben's stammering formality); the "Is that a challenge?" beat is a genuine character turn for Ben, showing his quiet rebellion emerging organically; the closing image of the stolen watch and "I have your time" is a clever, thematically resonant payoff that ties kleptomania to romance. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally strains for effect ("crushed velvet" dusk, "molten bronze," "tapestry of illuminated domes") and the Gianicolo scene leans on stock romance beats — the windblown curl tuck, the "raw and unexpectedly quiet" softening. Alessandra risks being a manic-pixie archetype: her interiority stays opaque, though the prompt asked for enigma, so this is partly intentional. Ben's transformation from flustered pedant to willing accomplice is fast but earned through escalating beats. The kiss is somewhat predictable, and Enzo's "check your pockets" speech borders on over-explaining her character. Overall this is competent, engaging commercial fiction with a few clichés but real craft in pacing and dialogue. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The ambient hum of the life-support grid vibrates through the soles of my boots, a low, comforting purr that tells me The Last Outpost is still breathing. Outside the thick quartz observation bay, the Andromeda dust cloud swirls in slow-motion violet and bruised plum, cradling half a million tons of hollowed-out asteroid. Inside, it smells of toasted yeast, hot coolant, and the faint, sweet tang of unrefined deuterium. "Barnaby, if you don't recalibrate that manifold, your rig will vent half its thrust before you reach the outer drift," I say, sliding a bowl of fried crunch-grubs toward the grizzled prospector. "Ah, you worry too much, Nets," Barnaby grumbles into his beard, though he tucks a hand-welder into his vest pocket anyway. "She’s held together by spit and prayers for twenty cycles. She’ll hold twenty more." "And if she doesn't, I lose my best customer for bitter-ale," I reply, smiling easy. "I can't afford the hit to my margins." I have my flaws—I’m nosy, my temper flares if someone insults the soup, and I have a bad habit of keeping secrets that aren't mine to keep. But the station tolerates me because I keep the taps flowing, patch up their bar fights with field-grade dermaseal, and remember every miner's favorite poison. The hatch by the airlock hiss-clicks open, admitting a gust of recycled chill. A lone figure stumbles through, ducking low beneath the lintel. He’s an Amphid—tall, skin the iridescent gray of wet slate, his head crowned with a heavy mane of slender, suction-cupped tentacled dreads. Right now, they’re twitching erratically, half of them knotted together in a frizzy tangle that screams blind panic. He doesn't glance at the booth where the salvage crew is playing cards. He heads straight for the stool directly opposite my taps, his webbed boots scuffing heavily on the grated floor. He plops down, his shoulders caving in like a spent accordion. "Vega whisky, neat," he rasps, chest heaving. "Better make that a double." I reach below the rail, my fingers finding the heavy, square-shouldered bottle of Vega reserve without looking. I set down an amber tumbler, pour two fingers of the smoking, pale-gold liquid, and then grab my worn linen rag. Right between us, there’s an old scorch mark on the brass trim where a plasma flare once bit too deep. I rest the rag there and begin to wipe, small, steady circles. "Long shift out on the rocks?" I ask softly. He downs half the glass in one shuddering gulp, wincing as the peat and ethanol hit his gills. "I wasn't mining." "No?" I keep the rag moving. Circle, pause, circle. "You're flying the little *Sun-Skimmer*, aren't you? Out of dock six? Thought you were contracted for light-courier runs to the comms buoys." "Was," he says, staring into the amber dregs. He looks up, his secondary eyelids fluttering in rapid distress. "Contract's void. Everything's void." "Easy there," I say, leaning in just enough to keep my voice between him, me, and the glass. "You got a name, friend?" "Orren," he mutters. "Orren Vael." "Well, Orren, you’re safe at the Outpost. Take a breath. Tell me what blew your dreads in a twist." "We aren't safe," Orren whispers. He grips the counter, his knuckles blanching white against the dark wood. "Nobody on this rock is safe. Nets, right? That's what they call you?" "That's me." Wipe. Circle. Wipe. "And trust me, we get all sorts through that airlock. Pirates, tax hounds, brokenhearted surveyors. Outpost stands." "This isn't pirates," Orren says, his voice tight, dipping into a strained register that sets my teeth on edge. "I was running routine diagnostics on Relay Fourteen. The fringe relay. The one pointing out toward the black gulf, where there isn't supposed to be anything for three parsecs." "And?" "The beacon stopped pinging an hour before I arrived," he says. He finishes his glass, pushing it toward me. I refill it, just a single this time, without breaking the rhythm of my rag against the brass. "Relays die all the time, Orren. Solar grit shears the solar sails, or a micro-meteorite punches the core." "It didn't die," he snaps, then checks himself, glancing nervously toward Barnaby, who is currently laughing at someone's bad joke at the far end of the counter. Orren leans forward, his voice a frantic hiss. "It was swallowed." I pause my hand for a fraction of a second, then resume. "Swallowed." "Scrapped. Digested. Sucked into the ventral bay of a dreadnought running completely cold." A small, cold drop of adrenaline trickles down the back of my neck, but I keep my face carefully placid, the practiced mask of a woman who has poured drinks while orbital bombardments shook the ceiling. "A corporate gunship?" "No transponder," Orren says, his dreads quivering against his collar. "No thermal bloom. It was black plasteel, ancient design—pre-unification hull geometry, Nets. It had to be three kilometers from prow to stern." The rag halts. Pre-unification. "Did they see you?" I ask, my voice dropping lower. "I was running on auxiliary thrusters, drifted behind a Class-C chondrite chunk. I don't think their short-range picked me up." Orren swallows hard, his throat clicking. "But they aren't just sitting there. They deployed drones. Tens of thousands of little seeker-spiders, combing the belt." "Looking for ore?" "Looking for a frequency," he says, leaning so close I can smell the sour tang of ozone on his jacket. "I tapped their passive ping before I jumped. It was an interrogation pulse. Nets... they aren't scanning for minerals. They're broadcasting an old Vanguard retrieval sequence." My breath catches. The rag in my hand feels suddenly like lead. The Vanguard project had been erased thirty years ago. Buried under layers of red tape, dead admirals, and incinerated archives. It was the very thing that had sent me running to the farthest, ragged edge of Andromeda, trading a uniform and a cipher-key for an apron and a rag. "You shouldn't repeat that name," I say quietly, picking up the motion again. Circle. Circle. Grinding the cloth into the brass. "Not here. Not anywhere." "They're sweeping grid by grid," Orren insists, oblivious to the shift in my posture, his panic blinding him. "They're moving this way. If they hit the Outpost, they'll turn this station inside out to find whatever—or whoever—they're tracking. We have to tell the marshal. We have to evacuate." "And cause a mass stampede into a belt full of seeker drones?" I counter, keeping my tone dead-level. "You blow that whistle, three hundred miners panic, fire their thrusters all at once, and light up the sensor boards like a blooming nova." "Then what do we do?" His eyes are wide, glassy with terror. "Nets, what do we do?" I stare down at the dull reflection in the brass counter, the phantom of a life I thought was dead staring right back at me. "First," I say, tapping the rim of his glass, "you drink your whisky. Then, you're going to tell me the exact encryption code on that retrieval ping."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong cozy sci-fi chapter that hits nearly all of the prompt's requirements. The first-person, present-tense voice is maintained consistently throughout, and the prose has a warm, lived-in quality appropriate to the genre — the sensory details (toasted yeast, hot coolant, the scorch mark on the brass) establish the Outpost as a real, habitable place. The bartender's ritualistic rag-wiping is a nice recurring physical beat that grounds the dialogue scenes. The dialogue percentage is roughly at or slightly above the 60% target, and the exchanges are naturalistic, with distinct voices: Barnaby's gruff affection, Orren's escalating panic, Nets' careful dead-level control. The conflict — a mysterious pre-unification dreadnought broadcasting a Vanguard retrieval sequence, tied to Nets' hidden past — is established clearly and left unresolved, exactly as instructed. The final line ("you're going to tell me the exact encryption code on that retrieval ping") is a well-earned hook that recontextualizes Nets' backstory without dumping exposition. Strengths: the pacing is tight, the reveal escalates in believable increments, and Nets' practiced composure ("the practiced mask of a woman who has poured drinks while orbital bombardments shook the ceiling") shows rather than tells her history. The worldbuilding details (Amphids, secondary eyelids, gills, Class-C chondrites) are deployed economically. Weaknesses: the piece leans on some familiar genre furniture — the mysterious stranger with a terrible secret, the protagonist with a buried past in a black-ops project, the "you shouldn't repeat that name" beat. These are executed competently but are not surprising. Nets' flaws are stated rather than demonstrated ("I have my flaws—I'm nosy, my temper flares..."), a small tell-don't-show lapse, though her nosiness and secret-keeping do manifest in the plot. The stakes, while concrete, are somewhat generic military-mystery fare. A few phrases ("shoulders caving in like a spent accordion") flirt with overwriting but stay controlled. The emotional register is engaging but not deeply complex — tension and intrigue dominate; there's little interior conflict beyond the implied past. Overall this is polished, professional, well-structured genre fiction that fulfills the brief with confidence, held back from excellence mainly by its reliance on conventional tropes. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 76.6
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in New Orleans hits me like a wet wool blanket pulled straight from a dryer. It smells like stale chicory, river mud, and piss. The trucker who gave me a ride from Meridian had shoved me out at a red light somewhere near Canal Street with a muttered, *“End of the line, kid,”* before I could even grab my jacket off the floorboards. So now I’m standing on a cracked sidewalk, watching his rusted taillights bleed into the morning haze, shivering in eighty-degree heat. The left strap of my canvas backpack slips off my shoulder. I yank it back up. It immediately slides down again. The nylon webbing is frayed to hell, the plastic buckle snapped three months ago when I kicked it down the basement stairs back in Pigeon Forge. Pigeon Forge. God, even thinking the name makes my throat close up. Forty-eight hours ago, I was still sitting across the kitchen table from Mom, watching her face curdle. *“Concerning behavioural patterns,”* Mr. Harrison, the smug prick of a guidance counselor, had called it. He thought my acting out was about Dad leaving, or pot, or bad grades. He didn’t know shit. None of them did. Until I told them. *I’m trans,* I’d said, voice shaking like an autumn leaf in an exhaust fan. *I can’t do this girl routine anymore. I’m done.* Mom didn’t scream. That was the worst part. She just sighed, this heavy, disgusted sound, like I was a glass of spilled milk she didn’t want to wipe up, and said, *“I can’t deal with another one of your stunts, Taylor. You’re sick. We’ll call Harrison back on Monday.”* There was no Monday. Monday was thirty minutes to stuff three t-shirts, a binder, fifty-four dollars, and an apple into a broken bag, climbing out the bathroom window before the sun came up. Now I’m here. And I have exactly twenty-two dollars left. The strap slips again. I hitch it violently, glaring at a trio of tourists sipping neon-colored slushes out of plastic bongs. Nobody looks back. In Tennessee, I took up too much space just by breathing. Here, I’m invisible. It should feel like freedom, but it tastes like panic. My pulse is a hammer against my ribs. By midday, the humidity has turned my t-shirt into a second skin. My feet burn inside my beat-up Converse. I drift toward a patch of green surrounded by black iron spikes—Jackson Square, a sign says. The park is full of fortune tellers, brass players, and pigeons fat as bowling balls. I drop onto a low stone bench near an overgrown magnolia tree, pulling my knees to my chest. *What the fuck did you do, Taylor?* my brain screams. *You have no place to sleep. You don’t know anyone. What if they call the cops? What if Mom doesn’t even care enough to report you missing?* “You’re gonna get your shit boosted if you keep staring into space like that.” I jump, my head whipping around. Leaning against the brick pillar behind me is a kid who looks maybe seventeen, rail-thin, drowning in an oversized denim vest pinned with rusted bottle caps. Short, choppy black hair, dark circles bruised beneath sharp hazel eyes, and a strip of athletic tape wrapped tight around their right knuckles. “I’m not staring,” I snap, voice cracking slightly. Defensive, stupid, pure instinct. The kid snorts, pushing off the pillar and sauntering over. They drop onto the opposite end of the bench with the fluid grace of an alley cat. “Right. You’re just meditating on the beauty of concrete. Look at you. Fresh off the interstate. You reek of diesel and panic.” “I don’t reek of anything.” I hitch the backpack strap up my shoulder again. It slides right back down to my elbow. The kid watches the strap, amused. “That bag’s fighting you harder than a parish deputy. I’m Remy.” “Taylor.” “Taylor,” Remy repeats, tasting it. “No last name. Smart. Means you’re either dodging parents or parole.” “Parents,” I mutter, staring at my shoes. “Always the parents.” Remy digs into their vest pocket, pulls out a half-crushed pack of generic smokes, and sticks one between their lips without lighting it. Their hands are shaking just a fraction. I notice a faint, fresh scab slicing across their jawline. “Tennessee?” My head snaps up. “How did you—” “The twang, genius. You stretch your vowels like saltwater taffy.” Remy glances over my head, eyes scanning the square. Not casually, either. It’s a rhythmic, paranoid sweep—cop cars, park rangers, guys in dark glasses. “You got people here?” “No.” “Money?” “Some,” I lie. Remy laughs, a dry, raspy sound. “Right. You’re loaded. That’s why you’re sitting on a damp bench looking like a kicked puppy.” They lean in a little, lowering their voice. The amusement fades, replaced by something brittle and razor-sharp. “Listen to me, Taylor. New Orleans eats runaways for breakfast and spits out empty wallets and coroner reports. You wander Frenchmen Street after dark looking like a lost deer, somebody’s gonna offer you a warm bed, and by morning you’ll wish you were dead. You get me?” A chill cuts through the swampy heat. My stomach roils. “Why do you care?” Remy looks away, staring up into the twisted branches of the magnolia. Their jaw tightens, muscle ticking over that nasty scab. “Maybe I don’t. Maybe I just hate seeing tourists waste good bench space.” They pause, chewing on the unlit filter. “Or maybe three days ago I was the idiot sitting where you’re sitting, thinking I was out of the woods.” “What happened three days ago?” I ask, leaned forward despite myself. Remy’s eyes snap back to mine, dark and guarded. “Let’s just say there’s an angry foster dad in Baton Rouge with a fractured nose and my name on a missing persons file. And if he finds me before I make enough cash to catch a bus to Texas, I’m not going back to a group home. I’m going to a juvenile facility.” I swallow hard. Back home, my drama felt earth-shattering. My mom’s cold disgust, the silent rooms, the dread of existing in the wrong skin. But sitting next to Remy, the world suddenly feels massive, vicious, and completely indifferent to a sixteen-year-old’s heartbreak. “I came out,” I blurt out, not even knowing why. “To my family. They looked at me like I was a freak.” Remy doesn’t laugh. They take the cigarette out of their mouth and look at me—really look at me—taking in my oversized hoodie, my cropped hair, the desperate tension coiled in my spine. “You ain’t a freak,” Remy says, voice entirely devoid of sarcasm for the first time. “You’re just early. Takes people a long time to catch up. Most of ‘em never do.” The sun is dipping low now, casting long, bruised-purple shadows across the square. The brass band down the alley kicks into a loud, syncopated jazz standard, trumpets blaring into the dusk. Streetlamps hum to life, flickering against the falling dark. I’m terrified. Truly, deeply terrified. My ribs ache from my binder, my stomach is completely empty, and I don’t know where I’m going to close my eyes tonight. The strap of my backpack slips off my shoulder again. This time, Remy reaches over, grabs the loose nylon tail, and ties it into a tight, ugly square knot against the upper loop. “There,” Remy says, standing up and stretching their bruised hands toward the neon glow of the street. “Won’t slip now. Come on, Tennessee. I know a place behind an abandoned bakery that has an awning and dry cardboard. You buy me a po’boy with that ‘fortune’ you got, and I’ll make sure nobody shanks you before sunrise.” I look at the dark shadows lengthening between the trees, then look at Remy. I don’t know if I can trust them. I don’t know if I’ll survive this week. I reach back, test the knot. It holds. “Deal,” I say, and I follow them into the neon night.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece follows the prompt closely: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, a first day in New Orleans, a runaway with secrets (Remy), internal monologue, dialogue, and roughly the requested length. The voice is consistent—sardonic, anxious, teenage—and the mixed tense is handled competently, with past tense for backstory and present tense for the day itself. Strengths: The dialogue between Taylor and Remy is the highlight. Remy's lines ("You reek of diesel and panic," "New Orleans eats runaways for breakfast") are characterful and do double duty as world-building and warning. The recurring broken backpack strap is a well-chosen motif—its repair by Remy at the end is a small, earned gesture of trust that avoids melodrama. The mother's reaction ("like I was a glass of spilled milk she didn't want to wipe up") is a strong, specific image. Sensory grounding in New Orleans (humidity, chicory, Jackson Square, brass bands) is effective without becoming a travelogue. Weaknesses: Remy is somewhat stock—the wise street kid with a mysterious past and a heart of gold is a familiar archetype, and their rapid intimacy with a stranger strains believability slightly, though the piece acknowledges the risk ("I don't know if I can trust them"). Some images tip toward the overwrought: "voice shaking like an autumn leaf in an exhaust fan," "pigeons fat as bowling balls," "tastes like panic." The exposition dump about the coming-out scene, while necessary, is delivered in a fairly direct flashback that tells more than it needs to. The ending is cautiously hopeful rather than saccharine, which suits the material, but the "follows them into the neon night" beat is a touch romanticized for a story about the dangers facing runaways. Minor continuity: Taylor has $22, yet agrees to buy Remy a po'boy—plausible but slightly glossed over. Overall this is a polished, engaging chapter with a strong voice, good dialogue, and only mild clichés and occasional overwriting. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 76.6
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
It is a well-documented law of the post-collapse landscape that if a man sets out to find a three-quarter-inch rubber washer, the universe will inevitably provide him with six tons of twisted rebar, an agitated badger, and dysentery. Midas knew this. He had the knees of a man who knew this, both of which made the sound of a dry branch snapping whenever he stood up. "The drip," Midas said, squinting through the cracked windscreen of their home—a 1998 Volvo estate deeply embedded in an overgrown rhododendron bush—"is psychological warfare. It goes *plink*. Then it waits until you think it’s not going to *plink*, and then it *plinks*." On the passenger dashboard, Chewy stared ahead with the unblinking, glassy serenity of a creature whose manufacturer had long since dissolved into atomic dust. Chewy was, nominally, a koala. In practice, he was six inches of matted acrylic pelt stretched over a brass clockwork chassis, missing his left ear and possessing a small internal speaker that crackled like frying bacon. A small whir of gears groaned behind Chewy’s polyester ribs. "*Four out of five dentists recommend it,*" Chewy said in a tinny, cheerful baritone, "*for a brighter, whiter tomorrow.*" "Quite," said Midas. "So we go to the Megamart. We search the Plumbing and Sanitary aisle. We secure one rubber washer. We avoid the Skag-Benders, we do not look at the feral geese, and we return before noon. A surgical strike." Chewy’s head clicked thirty degrees to the left. A glass eye fell out, bounced off the gearstick, and vanished into the footwell. Midas sighed, retrieved an old bit of chewed twine, and tied the eye back into its socket. "A tactical masterpiece. Let’s move." *** The ruins of the Megamart sat in the valley like the carcass of a beached, corrugated-iron whale. The world had ended some seventy years prior—nobody was entirely certain why, though general consensus blamed an update to terms and conditions that went horribly wrong—and nature had spent the intervening decades attempting to turn consumer electronics into potting soil. "Step lightly," Midas murmured, picking his way through the shattered remains of Seasonal Gardening. "The floor is mostly ceiling here." Chewy, wedged firmly into the breast pocket of Midas’s canvas coat, emitted a faint hum. "*Reduces unsightly bloating,*” he confided to the empty air. The Plumbing aisle was located just past Homewares, which was currently occupied by a family of screech-owls who held very conservative views on trespassing. Midas skirted them with the agonizing caution of a man walking over dry cornflakes in church. He reached the promised land: Bin 42, Fasteners and Gaskets. Suspended over the bin was a skeletal display rack, groaning under the weight of three rusted water heaters that had fallen from the mezzanine in the Great Collapse of ’41 and were currently held aloft by nothing more than oxidized pride and a single strip of perished strapping. Directly beneath it lay a small, black rubber ring. The Grail. "You see?" Midas whispered, his hand trembling as he reached forward. "Civilization is simply a matter of applied—" A rusted spring snapped with the acoustics of a sniper rifle. Chewy’s internal mechanism buzzed violently. "*Batteries not included!*" he shrieked at ninety decibels. "*Warning: Choking hazard!*" The screech-owls took this personally. What followed was not so much an escape as an aggressive recalculation of physics. The water heaters came down with a subterranean roar that pulverized Bin 42 into a fine red powder. The collapse brought down an overhead ventilation duct, which in turn disturbed a hive of mud-wasps that had been peacefully living inside a display model bread-maker since the late autumn. Midas, running entirely on panic and brittle bone, sprinted toward the exit. He tripped over a vintage mop bucket, did a frantic, three-legged dance that would have won accolades in a more avant-garde era of theatre, and plunged headlong through the drywall into an adjacent, unexplored territory: *The Great Beyond*. It was the outdoor sporting goods section. More specifically, it was the fishing tackle department. "Ow," Midas observed, rolling over. "*Side effects may include nausea, dizziness, and sudden death,*" Chewy remarked from his pocket, his small speaker vibrating against Midas’s ribs. "Shut up, Chewy." "Is that someone in the hooks?" a voice called out from the dark. It was a wet, phlegmy voice. It belonged to the sort of man who wore three hats simultaneously and considered roadkill an under-leveraged breakfast option. Midas froze. He was tangled in forty yards of high-tensile nylon monofilament and had three barbed spinners embedded in the calf of his trousers. From the shadows emerged two Skag-Benders, wielding sharpened curtain rods and grinning with the desperate enthusiasm of people who hadn't had a hobby in three generations. "Fresh leather," the larger one grunted, eying Midas’s boots. Midas looked down at his breast pocket. Chewy was clicking furiously. "My companion is a demon," Midas said, his voice cracking only twice. "A god of the Before. He eats souls. And… and plaque." The Skag-Benders paused, squinting at the lumpy, one-eyed stuffed animal. Chewy gave a sudden, convulsive shudder. A gear slipped. A capacitor sparked. "*Wazzup!*" Chewy roared, with the full, unholy acoustic force of an ancient optical-disc soundbite. "*Snap into a Slim Jim! Just DO IT!*" A spark shot out of Chewy's nose, directly into a puddle of lawnmower fuel that had sat undisturbed since the turn of the century. *** They returned to the Volvo at dusk. Midas was missing his left boot, having abandoned it to the monofilament and the fire. He was covered in soot, had an owl feather stuck firmly to the bridge of his nose via congealed tree sap, and was limping in a way that suggested his pelvis was now held together mostly by polite disagreement. He slumped into the driver's seat and leaned his head against the steering wheel. Beside him, Chewy was placed back onto the dashboard. The koala’s fur was now predominantly charred black, his single glass eye was dangling against his cheek like a monocle, and his clockwork inside sounded like a pocket watch dropped into a blender. *Plink.* Midas did not move. *Plink.* Slowly, carefully, Midas opened his clenched fist. Sitting in his soot-stained palm was a washer. It was half-melted, distinctly oval-shaped, and roughly three times the diameter of the kitchen pipe. *Plink.* Chewy let out a final, dying rasp of static. A puff of grey smoke leaked from his mouth. "*Because...*" the bear whispered, fading into the eternal twilight of dead electronics, "*...you're worth it.*" Midas closed his eyes. "Tomorrow," he said to the ceiling, "we look for tape."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a competent and often funny Pratchett pastiche that hits most of the brief's beats: deliberation at home base (the Volvo), a mission (the washer) that goes sideways in escalating fashion, and a return home worse for wear. The comic voice is well sustained—dry, wry, footnote-adjacent asides ("the knees of a man who knew this"), and a fondness for absurd institutional detail (the collapse blamed on a terms-and-conditions update). Chewy's glitching advertising slogans are a genuinely clever device: the koala speaks only in corrupted marketing soundbites, which yields excellent punchlines ("Batteries not included!", "Because... you're worth it") and gives the ending a bittersweet, earned payoff. Strengths: the prose is economical and rhythmically confident; imagery is vivid and specific (the Megamart as a beached corrugated-iron whale, water heaters held aloft by "oxidized pride"); the escalation in the Plumbing aisle is well-structured slapstick; the dialogue, while mostly one-sided, is sharp and characterful. The final "we look for tape" line lands the Pratchett-style resigned coda nicely. Weaknesses: the plot is essentially a single comic set-piece and fairly predictable in its trajectory—mission goes wrong, chaos, fire, return. The Skag-Benders are thinly sketched and dispatched too easily via an unearned deus ex machina (Chewy's spark igniting fuel resolves the threat off-page, literally with a scene break). Midas is a consistent type but not deeply nuanced; the emotional register stays at "wry amusement" with only a light touch of pathos at the end. Some jokes are stock ("Wazzup," "Just DO IT") and the badger/dysentery opening promises more chaos than the story delivers. The washer being half-melted and the wrong size is a good ironic beat, though the drip's persistence is slightly convenient. Overall: a polished, entertaining, professional-grade comic short that falls short of masterpiece only through predictability of structure and slight thinness of character. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the door didn’t just ring; it shrieked as the heavy oak was slammed shut against the Welsh drizzle. Outside, across the rain-slicked cobbles of the square, two figures with telephoto lenses skidded on the wet slate, cursing into the grey mist. Inside, Julian Fox collapsed back against the shut door, chest heaving beneath his drenched cashmere overcoat. He pulled off his dark glasses with a theatrical flourish, ran a hand through artfully ruined dark curls, and offered the empty shop a breathless, cinematic smirk. “Narrow thing,” he murmured. From behind the counter, half-buried behind a stack of local historical gazetteers, a dry voice replied, “Mind the umbrella stand. It’s Victorian, and it bites.” Julian blinked, adjusting his eyes to the amber gloom of the shop. She sat on a high stool, wearing an oversized cable-knit sweater the colour of moss and a pencil tucked behind an ear. She didn’t look up from her ledger. She didn't drop her pen. She didn't even gasp. Julian’s smile tightened by a fraction of a millimetre. A tiny, familiar tremor of panic—the cold little voice that whispered *they’re not looking at you*—grazed his ribs. He deployed the Fox Smile: the one that had carried him through three West End revivals and two blockbuster franchises. Slow, slightly lopsided, wickedly warm. “Terribly sorry about the intrusion,” he said, stepping forward. He let the resonant, velvet baritone do the heavy lifting. “A pack of hounds out there. Mind if I take sanctuary among the paperbacks for twenty minutes? I’m Julian, by the way.” The woman finally looked up. Her eyes were a sharp, hazel grey, completely unreadable. Inwardly, Gwenna’s heart did an absurd, terrifying leap into her throat. *Julian Fox.* It was ridiculous. He looked absurdly, offensively good in the dim Welsh rainlight—the jawline carved by someone who clearly took themselves very seriously, the scent of expensive bergamot and wet wool cutting right through the dust. Her pulse hammered in her wrists, but five generations of stubborn mountain stock refused to let her show it. She laid her pen down with deliberate slowness. “Twenty minutes is fine, Julian By-The-Way. Browsing fee is five pounds, or you actually buy a book.” Julian paused mid-stride. He gave an airy laugh, testing the waters. “A cover charge? For me?” “For anyone whose boots are currently tracking slate-mud onto my runner,” she said mildly. Julian glanced down. He was indeed leaving damp footprints. A hot prickle rushed up the back of his neck. *She doesn’t know who I am,* he thought, horrified. *Or worse, she does, and she finds me boring.* “Right,” he said, drawing nearer to the counter, leaning an elbow on the scarred mahogany. He tilted his head, holding her gaze with practiced, devastating intensity. “Let’s start over. I’m seeking refuge. You’re the enigmatic guardian of… ancient wisdom. Tell me, do you treat all your paying customers like errant schoolboys, or did I do something specifically to earn the honour?” Gwenna felt the heat rising in her collarbones. His eyes were entirely too bright, his presence crowding the small space between the counter and the poetry section. It made her want to smooth her hair; instead, she crossed her arms tightly over her chest. “I find the schoolboy approach keeps egos from bruising the woodwork,” she said. “Particularly the imported ones.” Julian’s charming smirk flickered. He straightened up, his velvet façade fraying just enough to reveal the restless, insecure boy beneath. “Imported? I’ll have you know my grandmother was from the Rhondda.” “Was she?” Gwenna tilted her head, her gaze drifting unimpressed down his immaculate Italian lapels. “Did she teach you to stand about posturing while dripping rainwater all over an 1890 edition of George Borrow?” He stepped back as if stung, his hands going up defensively. “I’m not posturing. I was merely… making conversation.” He rubbed the back of his neck, the theatricality suddenly draining away, replaced by an earnest, exasperated pout. “Look, do you really not—? Never mind. It doesn't matter.” Gwenna almost smiled. The sudden collapse of his swagger was devastatingly endearing. She fought the urge to soften, her fingers digging into the wool of her sleeves. “Tea?” she asked. Julian blinked. “What?” “I’ve a kettle on the back stove. You look like a drowned spaniel.” “A drowned— I am an artist,” he muttered, though the offended edge in his voice lacked any real bite. He watched her slip off the stool. “Milk, please. No sugar.” She disappeared into the back alcove. Julian stood in the quiet shop, listening to the clatter of mugs, feeling strangely off-kilter. Usually, by minute three, people were asking for selfies or looking flustered. She was entirely immune. It drove him mad. It made him want to stand on the counter and recite Shakespeare until she looked at him with something resembling awe. His eyes fell to the desk. Beside her ledger lay a wooden tackle box, open to reveal brass scales, small camel-hair brushes, a pocket microscope, and several neatly labeled wax-paper packets. Julian leaned closer. He frowned, his curiosity piqued. He reached out and nudged one of the packets with a finger. When Gwenna returned, balancing two mismatched mugs, she found him bent double over the desk, nose practically touching the wood. “Careful,” she said sharply. “Those are delicate.” “*Boletus edulis*?” Julian asked without looking up. He pointed a long, slender finger at a pale, dried cross-section. “No, wait. Pores are too yellow for a young cep. Is that… a birch bolete? Look at the scrobiculations on the stipe.” Gwenna froze, nearly slopping Earl Grey onto the floorboards. She set the mugs down with a soft clack. “*Leccinum scabrum*,” she corrected, her voice losing its guarded dry edge. “Harvested near the reservoir on Tuesday.” Julian looked up, his eyes wide and completely stripped of his earlier artifice. “You’re a forager.” “I am,” she said, caught off guard. “Don't tell me you eat wild fungi. Hollywood actors only consume activated almonds and sunlight, surely.” Julian scoffed, picking up his mug and ignoring the barb. “Hollywood can keep its almonds. There’s nothing on earth like finding a flush of chanterelles hidden under beech leaf litter after a hard frost. My uncle kept a cottage in Sussex. Used to drag me out at dawn with a wicker basket and an Opinel knife.” He leaned in, the actor forgotten, replaced by genuine zeal. “Tell me you have a spot for horn of plenty around here. I’ve been craving *Craterellus cornucopioides* for three months, and the hotel chef in Cardiff looked at me like I’d asked him to cook a shoe.” Gwenna stared at him. The arrogant veneer was utterly gone; his face was open, animated, lit from within by pure, unadulterated nerdiness. Her stomach did that dangerous flip again, much more violently this time. “Black trumpets?” she whispered, leaning forward over the counter despite herself. “Two miles up the valley. Under the old oaks by the stream.” “You’re lying.” Julian was inches from her now, leaning over the display, his gaze locked onto hers. The space between them crackled with an entirely new, electric friction. “They’re nearly impossible to spot in the wet.” “Not if you know how to look for the shadows instead of the caps,” Gwenna murmured. She swallowed, suddenly excruciatingly aware of the gold flecks in his dark eyes, and how close his mouth was to hers. Her breath hitched. Julian saw it—the slight parting of her lips, the subtle flush that climbed the graceful curve of her throat. For once in his life, he didn't feel the smug thrill of victory. He just felt an ache, sudden and heavy, right in the center of his chest. “Show me,” he said, his voice dropping to a rough, genuine whisper. “When the rain stops. Take me with you.” Gwenna held his gaze, her defensive walls crumbling into the quiet scent of damp paper and Earl Grey. “Maybe,” she said softly, picking up her pencil again, though her fingers trembled just enough for him to see. “If you buy a book first.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene delivers on nearly all prompt requirements: a famous actor (Julian Fox) ducks into a Welsh bookstore to escape paparazzi, meets the owner (Gwenna), and their dialogue crackles with unspoken chemistry. Julian is written as a rogue with a fragile ego—his internal panic at not being recognized, his need to be liked, and the visible fraying of his charm offensive are all effectively rendered. Gwenna's outward immunity masking inward fluster is handled well, largely through physical tells (trembling fingers, heat in her collarbones, pulse hammering) that show rather than merely tell, though there is some direct interiority narration ("her heart did an absurd, terrifying leap") that borders on telling. The strongest structural choice is the mushroom-foraging pivot. It derails the charm offensive in a believable, specific, and creative way, gives both characters genuine expertise and vulnerability, and produces the scene's best dialogue ("You're lying." / "Not if you know how to look for the shadows instead of the caps"). The double meaning lands elegantly. The final line, "If you buy a book first," calls back to the opening browsing-fee joke, giving the scene a satisfying, understated close that earns its light positivity rather than imposing it. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally strains—"cinematic smirk," "wickedly warm," "resonant, velvet baritone" are romance-genre stock phrases, and the interior monologue italic thoughts are a slightly amateurish device. Some descriptions of the attraction are formulaic ("gold flecks in his dark eyes," "the space between them crackled"). Gwenna's POV intrusions occasionally explain the subtext rather than trusting it. The voices are distinct but Julian's dialogue occasionally tips into self-parody. The ~1000-word target is met and the pacing is tight; no meandering. The imagery of the Welsh setting (slate, drizzle, cobbles, damp paper, Earl Grey) is well-textured and specific. Emotionally, the piece is engaging and achieves genuine complexity: Julian's ache being non-smug is a nice subversion of his own pattern. The transformation—both dropping their guards over fungi—is gradual enough to feel earned within one scene.
