+ Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**INCIDENT LOG / PERSONAL STATEMENT: SCP-8419-A** **AUTHOR:** Dr. Jeremy Vance, Senior Researcher (Sub-Level 4, Site-44) **STATUS:** Active Containment Review / Psychological Quarantine *** The first note appeared on November 3rd, tucked neatly beneath my optical microscope. It was written on standard Foundation-issue grid paper using a Pilot G2 0.5mm pen—the only writing utensil I have used for a decade. The handwriting was unmistakably mine, complete with the slight leftward tilt of the *t*-crossings and the truncated tail on the *g* that my fifth-grade teacher tried and failed to correct. > *Jeremy.* > *On the 14th, at 03:14, Sector-4 primary airlock seal will decompress. Do not authorize the secondary nitrogen purge. If you flood the corridor, you kill everyone who tried to breathe. Break the glass on Manual Override C instead. Memorize this.* I stared at it for three full minutes before calling Site Security. My initial assumption was a breach of operational security or a juvenile prank by one of the junior researchers on SCP-6192's containment team. However, when Head of Security Miller pulled the surveillance feeds for my office, the footage told a different story. At 08:14:22, the camera experienced a severe frame drop. Exactly 1.14 seconds of footage vanished into a wash of gray, digital snow. When the feed snapped back to normal at 08:14:24, the paper was on my desk. I had been sitting there the entire time, my eyes lowered to my terminal, completely oblivious. Miller classified the note as a Class-2 Temporal Hazard and had it transferred to Chrono-Spatial Analysis. I underwent a mandatory four-hour cognitohazard screening. The results returned clean: no mnestic decay, no latent memetic hooks, no neurochemical irregularities. The ink on the paper was Foundation stock, but mass spectrometry showed an isotopic decay signature indicating the paper had been manufactured approximately three weeks in the future. Two days later, the second note arrived. I was writing up a quarterly review. I blinked—just a momentary flutter of the eyelids—and felt something scrape against the side of my palm. > *The override didn’t work. Why didn’t you check the manual crank? It was seized with rust. Dr. Aris wasn’t infected; the blood on her collar was transmission fluid from the drone. We threw her into the incinerator for nothing. Stop looking at the cameras. They can’t see the seam.* My heart hammered against my ribs. I immediately dialed Security. The review was identical: at 14:02:51, the wide-angle camera above my office door glitched for 0.89 seconds, broadcasting a burst of high-frequency white noise that fried the site's local audio feed. When the image stabilized, the second note was pinned beneath my hand. What made my skin crawl was the content. Dr. Aris was our lead biophysicist. She was currently in the cafeteria eating lunch. But more importantly: there was no drone in Sector-4. We had never used maintenance drones in that wing. When I pointed this out to Miller, the inquiry shifted. "Temporal displacement often features divergent causal branches," Miller told me through the intercom of the quarantine cell they moved me to. "Or it isn't temporal at all." "Meaning?" I asked, my palms sweating against the cold steel table. "SCP-7740 is three doors down from your lab," he said coldly. "Its psychic radius is dormant, but its whole nature is parasitic cognitive mimicry. It feeds on anticipated grief. It might be manufacturing a future to drive you into an actionable panic." By November 9th, the Foundation had me under twenty-four-hour continuous surveillance. Four high-speed cameras, each operating on independent power supplies, pointed directly at the small metal desk in my quarters. Two armed guards stood at the threshold, their eyes locked on me. At 19:40:02, all four cameras simultaneously spiked with static. The guards' tactical radios emitted a deafening screech of electromagnetic interference that caused both men to flinch and clasp their helmets. The disruption lasted 1.6 seconds. When the monitors cleared, three sheets of paper lay scattered across the linoleum floor. The handwriting had deteriorated. The lines were jagged, pressing so hard into the pulp that the paper was torn in several places. > *IT DIDN’T COME FROM THE CELLS.* > *It was in the ventilation before the sirens even started. We forgot that Site-44 has an open-air intake on the north ridge. Why did you seal the vault when the sky was already red? The D-Class with the scarred ear isn't real. He has no teeth behind his tongue. Jeremy, look at your knuckles. Look at the scabs.* I scrambled off the cot and held my hands up to the fluorescent light. My skin was smooth, pale, unmarked. There were no scabs. Site-44 was buried three hundred meters beneath a salt flat in Nevada; there was no north ridge, no open-air intake, and no sky to turn red. "It's a reality bleed," I shouted at the security lens in the ceiling, my voice cracking. "Or I'm losing my mind! Sedate me! Class-A amnestics, wipe the last two weeks, just wipe it!" Dr. Aris's voice came through the speaker. She sounded calm, clinical, and horrifyingly distant. "We can't do that, Jeremy. If this is a legitimate precognitive tether, amnesticizing you could sever the anchor and cause an uncontained temporal collapse. Or worse, it could ensure whatever occurs happens without warning. You stay put." "The notes contradict reality!" I screamed, slamming my fists onto the steel desk. "She’s talking about things that don't exist! *I'm* talking about things that don't exist!" "Or things that don't exist *yet*," she replied softly. The final note did not arrive on my desk. On the night of November 13th, exhausted beyond coherence, I was lying on the cot, staring unblinkingly at the ceiling camera. I was determined to watch it happen. I held my breath until my lungs burned. The room flickered. It wasn't a glitch on a screen. For a single, terrifying heartbeat, the physical world dropped its frames. The light ceased to exist, replaced by a suffocating, metallic static that hummed in the marrow of my teeth. When my vision returned, my hand was clamped shut. Inside my fist was a scrap of bloody cardstock. My fingers were trembling so violently I could barely unfold it. > *The breach isn't a monster, Jeremy. The breach is the protocol. When the alarm sounds at 03:14, they are going to lock you in this room because they think you're the vector. They are going to purge the oxygen. You have to break the camera. Use the glass to cut the mag-lock wire. If you don't, you die here, scribbling backward into the dark, hoping one of these lies makes you run.* I looked up at the camera dome. On the other side of the reinforced glass, Miller and Aris were staring at me through the observation window. Their faces were dead, blank masks. I glanced at the digital wall clock. 03:12. I looked down at my hands. The pen was in my pocket. And across my knuckles, raw and fresh, were three bleeding scabs I had never seen before.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly effective piece of SCP-formatted fiction that executes the prompt's requirements with notable skill. The first-person past-tense perspective is maintained throughout, and the interspersed notes escalate convincingly from composed instruction to desperate incoherence, exactly as requested. Strengths: The escalation structure is well-managed—each note arrives with a plausible delivery mechanism (camera glitches, frame drops, physical manifestation), and the deterioration of the handwriting mirrors the deterioration of the future self's sanity. The central ambiguity is preserved skillfully: the Foundation's counter-hypothesis (SCP-7740's parasitic cognitive mimicry) is given real weight, and the isotopic dating of the paper is a nice touch of institutional rigor. The contradictions with known reality (the north ridge, the open-air intake, the D-Class with no teeth) do genuine work—they keep the reader oscillating between "temporal anomaly" and "psychological manipulation/psychosis" right up to the end. The ending is the piece's boldest choice: the scabs appearing on the narrator's knuckles retroactively validates the note's most deranged claim, collapsing the ambiguity into horror while leaving the temporal mechanics unresolved. The final image—03:12 on the clock, the pen in the pocket, the implication that the narrator is the one who will write the notes—is a satisfying loop that recontextualizes everything without over-explaining. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally leans on familiar SCP clichés (Class-A amnestics, cognitohazard screening, the salt-flat Nevada site) but these are genre-appropriate rather than amateurish. Some of the technical detail (mass spectrometry on paper, precise glitch durations) borders on filler, though it also builds the clinical voice. The dialogue is functional but slightly expository—Miller and Aris exist mostly to voice hypotheses. Aris's "Or things that don't exist yet" is a bit on-the-nose. The emotional register is somewhat narrow: fear and dread are well-rendered, but the narrator's interiority beyond terror (grief for Dr. Aris, professional identity, relationships) is thin, which slightly limits emotional complexity. The piece is also more plot-machine than character study; Dr. Vance is a vessel for the anomaly rather than a fully rounded person. The prose is clean, controlled, and appropriately clinical with well-timed bursts of visceral imagery ("hummed in the marrow of my teeth"). It avoids purple excess. Pacing is tight; there is no meandering. The word count lands near the 1000-word seed. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7842 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** All known instances of SCP-7842 are to be welded shut, enclosed within reinforced concrete vestibules, and monitored by remote surveillance. Condemned municipal, industrial, and residential properties scheduled for demolition must be surveyed for anomalous apertures prior to clearance. Under zero-lux testing environments, researchers are instructed to note that a faint glow escapes through the door’s edges in complete darkness; light emissions must be cataloged for flux variances. Under no circumstances are personnel below Level 4 clearance permitted to access recovered indices. **Description:** SCP-7842 designates a recurring phenomenon involving the spontaneous manifestation of identical, unmarked doors within uninhabited or derelict structures worldwide. Instances are constructed of seamless, cold-rolled carbon steel, lacking keyholes, latches, or external hardware. Despite the absence of a visible light source within their structural margins, when an instance is plunged into total darkness, an amber luminescence bleeds consistently from the microscopic seams between the door and frame. Opening an instance requires an outward pull along the flush seam. SCP-7842 instances do not connect to the expected architecture of their host buildings. Instead, all confirmed apertures access a singular, continuous, non-Euclidean subterranean megastructure designated SCP-7842-1. SCP-7842-1 is an archive of indeterminate scale, constructed predominantly of black basalt, unpolished bronze, and vaulted acoustic tiles. The interior extends downward and horizontally for at least several hundred kilometers, organized into concentric tiers of filing stacks, microfilm carousels, and climate-controlled storage vaults. Atmospheric conditions remain constant at 9°C and 18% humidity. Recovered materials within SCP-7842-1 document historical, sociological, and technological milestones of a technologically advanced global human civilization predating the current Holocene epoch. The catalog outlines an interconnected global population exceeding nine billion, governed by a technocratic administrative body. Every historical line terminates abruptly at an arbitrary baseline date approximately 12,000 years ago, following an event repeatedly designated only as "Unscheduled Total Extraction" or "The Breached Lattice." No specific anomaly is identified; rather, the logs describe the systematic collapse of containment protocols across twenty-two thousand regional facilities over a period of seventy-two hours. Throughout the recovered documentation, this precursor entity is referred to as *The Panopticon Assembly*. Cross-referencing reveals that organizational bylaws, containment philosophies, classification metrics, and internal jargon within the Assembly are identical to modern Foundation doctrine. *** ### Exploration Log 7842-Alpha **Date:** October 14, 2024 **Lead:** Captain Marcus Vance (MTF Zeta-9 "Mole Rats") **Team:** Specialist Nolan Cruz, Field Archivist Dr. Laura Aris **Entry Point:** SCP-7842 Instance-19 (Abandoned textile refinery, Charleroi, Belgium) The breach-seal of Instance-19 yielded under hydraulic pressure. Once the exterior floodlights were deactivated, the perimeter of the frame cast a faint, amber radiance across the factory floor before swinging outward. The team descended a central spiral staircase descending approximately sixty meters into Archive Tier 04. The air smelled of dry cellulose and burnt vacuum tubes. Rows of iron shelving extended beyond the throw of their tactical lanterns, lost in a cold, blue-black haze. Suspended walkways hung over deep vertical chasms, their guide cables taut and vibrating with distant, subsonic frequencies. "Look at the floor," Specialist Cruz muttered, sweeping his rifle-mounted light across the flagstones. "Fresh tracks." Parallel tracks in the dust led toward the southern mezzanine. Vance signaled for silence, leading the unit between two fifty-foot shelving units labeled *GEOGRAPHICAL REDISTRIBUTION: POST-COLLAPSE (NULL).* Ahead, harsh halogen light spilled from an intersecting aisle. The team approached the corner. Dr. Aris paused, adjusting her optical recorder. Within the aisle, three humanoid figures worked in total silence. The entities were clad in bulky, slate-gray hazardous material suits featuring mirrored, convex visors and closed-circuit rebreathers. Using pneumatic shearing tools, the figures were systematically severing entire shelf segments, loading massive bundles of vellum ledgers and magnetic spools into high-density composite transit cases. "Foundation salvage?" Cruz whispered over local comms. "They aren’t wearing our patches." Captain Vance stepped around the bulkhead, raising his weapon to low-ready. "This is Mobile Task Force Zeta-9. Cease operations and step away from the containers." The three figures froze simultaneously. They did not raise hands or vocalize. One entity dropped an unsealed filing ledger; the second slammed the latch on a transit case. Before Vance could advance, the entity nearest the wall pulled a wall-mounted brass lever. A pneumatic depressurization valve vented overhead, flooding the corridor with a dense, opaque aerosol of suspended talc and freon. Cruz fired two warning rounds into the ceiling, but the sound of boots scrambled rapidly down the metal gangway. By the time the exhaust fans cleared the air, the entities had vanished. An emergency bulkhead door at the end of the aisle had been welded shut from the far side with a high-temperature magnesium torch. Dr. Aris knelt by the dropped ledger. "They left this." She lifted the volume. The leather binding was cracked with age. The header, embossed in faded gold foil, bore the emblem of three inward-facing arrows surrounding three dots—the Foundation crest—encircled by the words *THE PANOPTICON ASSEMBLY: SPECIAL ANOMALOUS COHORT.* Aris flipped to a marked page. She stopped breathing. "What is it?" Vance asked, scanning the dark rafters. "It’s an administrative dossier," Aris said, her voice shaking. "Classified Level 4 personnel registry. Field Operations Division." She turned the book toward Vance’s light. A silver-halide photograph was affixed to the upper right corner. The photograph depicted Captain Marcus Vance, clean-shaven, dressed in a high-collared woolen tunic bearing the rank of Third Surveyor. The document was dated *14th Century, Cycle IV (Julian equivalent: October 1341).* The fingerprints recorded on the bottom margin were an identical match to Vance’s standard biometric profile. "That’s impossible," Vance said. "That’s a forgery. Let’s keep moving." The team proceeded two hundred meters inward to the Tier 04 Central Administrative Hub, a circular rotunda dominated by dead cathode-ray terminals and mahogany desks. On the central desk lay an anomalous discrepancy: a modern, active Foundation-issue biometric data pad. Its battery was at 94%. Specialist Cruz secured the perimeter while Dr. Aris approached the terminal. The screen was unlocked. "Someone was just here," Aris whispered. "They bypassed the local security terminal using a hardwired override." "Read the log," Vance ordered. The terminal display showed an active query into the deep-storage records of *Cycle V*, cross-referenced with modern demographic shifts. The bottom of the screen displayed an authorization header: ``` TERMINAL SESSION ACTIVE CLEARANCE CONFIRMED: OVERSEER LEVEL 5 IDENT: O5-08 (Verified via retinal and vascular scan) OVERRIDE CODE: 08-BLACKTHORN-RECOLLECTION SESSION START: 42 MINUTES AGO ``` Beneath the clearance banner sat a series of retrieved and subsequently deleted files. Only a single system note remained unpurged in the local cache: > *Consensus achieved (11-2). The reclamation teams must accelerate extraction of all pre-failure records concerning the Lattice. Cycle VII is demonstrating identical drift signatures to Cycle VI. The staff must not learn that the quarantine has failed before, or that we are the ones who cleared the board.* > > *Ensure the doors remain shut when the lights go out.* In the darkness beyond the rotunda, the faint amber glow from dozens of unseen doorways began to pulse in unison, like the steady, slow respiration of an animal waiting to wake. Vance lowered his weapon, looked at the photograph of his own face from seven centuries prior, and gave the order to retreat.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a well-executed SCP entry that fulfills essentially every element of the prompt: identical unmarked doors in abandoned buildings worldwide, an architecturally impossible archive, a precursor global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure ("The Breached Lattice"), an organization mirroring the Foundation ("The Panopticon Assembly"), personnel files of current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-suited entities removing records who flee when approached, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits (the active terminal logged to O5-08). The third-person exploration team perspective and recovered document excerpts are both present. Length lands close to the 1000-word seed. Strengths: The prose is disciplined and clinical in the containment/description sections, then shifts effectively to tense field-log narration. The amber glow in darkness is a nice recurring motif, paying off in the final image of pulsing doorways "like the slow respiration of an animal waiting to wake." The system note from the O5 terminal is the strongest single beat — "we are the ones who cleared the board" and "Ensure the doors remain shut when the lights go out" deliver genuine dread economically. The Vance dossier reveal is handled with good pacing, and his denial ("That's a forgery. Let's keep moving") is a believable, human deflection. Weaknesses: Dialogue is functional but occasionally stiff and expository ("It's an administrative dossier... Classified Level 4 personnel registry. Field Operations Division."). "She stopped breathing" is a cliché. The hazmat entities' escape via aerosol and welded bulkhead is competent but the confrontation resolves a bit too conveniently. Some worldbuilding details (twenty-two thousand facilities, seventy-two hours) are efficient but read as texture rather than earned revelation. The ending's pulsing doors edge toward the overwrought but is largely earned. Characters are thin — Vance gets a flicker of interiority, Cruz and Aris are functional archetypes — which is genre-appropriate but limits emotional complexity. The piece is coherent, never meanders, and maintains consistent tone throughout. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 74.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air of Oth-Sula tasted of dry shale and unsprouted grain. It was heavy in the lung, thick with the exhalations of two divergent branches of a tree that had forgotten its common root. Solin had left his comm-bead on the dresser beneath the glass lamp. To walk unaccompanied was an infraction of the Third Concord, but the Concord had been written by men who lived in pressurized pods and thought of planets as equations to be balanced with ledger-ink. In the lower market of the Lower Terrace, there were no equations. The briefings had termed them the *Stilt-born* and the *Lithic*. Here, in the damp shadows beneath the aqueduct, they called one another simply *neighbor* or *thief*, depending on the price of meal. The Lithic men and women—low-slung, with barrel-ribs hardened against the sulfur-seeps of the deep troughs—squatted on their haunches, their broad, pale palms splayed upon rough flagstones. Leaning over them were the long-limbed Graces, their skin the blue-grey of skimmed milk, ribs curving beneath tunics like the wicker frames of kites. According to the Ministry of Cohesion, these two could not share air without bloodshed. The official documents spoke of ancestral vendettas, of biological incompatibilities that curdled into pogroms every sixth solstice. Yet Solin watched a Grace woman with fingers six inches long gently mend the collar of a Lithic boy whose neck was as thick as an oak bole. She did not flinch; the boy did not snarl. He merely held a spindle for her while she worked. Beside them, hung upon line after line of hempen twine, were the bolts of cloth. Solin stopped, his fingers hovering above a strip of coarse weave. It was dyed in a pigment that troubled the optic nerve—not purple, not ochre, but an unstable, shifting twilight that seemed to drink the pale sunlight and return it as the color of bruised slate. It came, he had heard, from the gall-secretion of the deep-trench sponges, an organic compound containing no carbon, impossible to replicate in the synthesis chambers of Earth. Beside it hung yards of a color like burning tin, cold yet luminous. A woman with four pupils watched him from behind the stall, her breath misting between sharp, translucent teeth. "You smell of iron and boiled water, small traveler," she said. Her dialect was a slurry of old Terran and the clipped clicks of the trough-dwellers. "I am looking," Solin said. "You look with your ears back," she observed, folding a hem of the tin-colored wool. "Like a goat that expects the wolf. The wolves here sit on councils, Offworlder. They do not buy cloth." When Solin returned to the Consulate compound through the side cistern-gate, Councilor Vane was already waiting in the vestibule, his hands tucked into the severe folds of his gray fleece coat. "Forty minutes," Vane said, not looking up from his slate. "The monitoring grid flagged your absence at the third checkpoint. The High Commissioner is having an attack of the liver, and I have had to explain to two under-secretaries why our junior attache was wandering the meat-gutters like an escaped steer." "The streets are quiet, Councilor," Solin said, stripping his dust-cloak. "The Lithics and the Graces are trading salt and spindle-work. There were no riots." "There are always riots," Vane snapped, turning his cold, bird-like eye upon Solin. "If not today, then next month when the melt begins. Do not confuse a lull in slaughter with peace, Solin. It is an offworld disease, this sentimental ethnography. You have compromised our leverage before the talks have even begun." Vane thrust a vellum dossier into Solin's chest. "You will not go back to your quarters. Minister Gray has requested an audience. He is at the High Conservatory. You will go now." "Gray?" Solin hesitated. "The Minister of Science?" "The *titular* Minister of Science," Vane corrected with a thin, bitter curl of his lip. "A man who could not tell an amino acid from a turnip, but who controls three seats in the Directorate and every deep-core drilling permit south of the ice. He wants to measure you. Do not let him find you short." The High Conservatory was warm, kept at an artificial, humid eighty degrees to preserve a collection of dead-world mosses that rotted slowly under glass bells. Orlaith Gray sat behind a low table of petrified wood. He was a Grace by blood, but one whose lineage had been smoothed out by wealth and selective breeding; his height was contained, his skin bleached to the pale tone of almond meal, his eyes small and dark like currants pressed into dough. He was eating pickled plums with a small silver fork. "The young man from the ship," Gray said, without rising. "Sit, Envoy. The chairs are built for your pelvis, not mine. They will not pinch." Solin sat, keeping his spine straight, his hands rested flat upon his knees in the traditional posture of an Ekumen neutral. "Minister Gray." "You were in the Trough Gate," Gray said, chewing slowly. "Looking at rags." "I was looking at the weave," Solin said. "The Graces spin the warp; the Lithics tread the fuller’s earth. It seems a delicate balance to break for the sake of the sulfur concession." Gray laughed—a dry, clicking sound that died quickly in the moss-heavy air. "You think like an islander. You look at two hands clasping and you think, *ah, love.* You do not see that the left hand is holding the right hand down so the throat may be cut." "The boy whose tunic was mended had no knife at his throat," Solin said quietly. "He will," said Gray. He laid his fork aside. His dark, currant eyes fixed on Solin with sudden, predatory focus. "The Lithics are growing thicker in the skull, Solin. The lung-cavity deepens with every generation down in the salt-workings. In two centuries, their children will not be able to breathe this air without compressors. And my people—my cousins on the ridges—their marrow is turning to lace. We are no longer the same genus. Do your texts from Earth tell you what happens when two distinct species contest the same pasture?" "They tell me that species is a fiction invented by taxonomists," Solin replied, holding the Minister’s stare. "And that human beings have never required a biological distinction to slaughter one another. But they also tell me that trade follows the thread, not the bone." Gray leaned forward, resting his sharp elbows on the petrified wood. His greyish skin stretched taut over his cheekbones. "You are very young. It is a terrible disadvantage in an envoy. You believe that because something is natural, it is permanent. We have engineered ourselves into two cages, Offworlder. My ministry exists not to discover what is true, but to invent the reasons why the strong cage must lock the weak one." "And which are you, Minister?" Solin asked, his voice low, steady as stone. "The lock, or the key?" For three seconds, the room was so quiet that Solin could hear the slow, rhythmic dripping of the condensation against the glass bells. Gray did not flinch, but his fingers drifted back toward the silver fork, turning it over once, twice, against the dark grain of the wood. A smile, thin as a razor's edge, touched the corners of his mouth. "A dangerous question, Envoy," Gray murmured. "Let us hope, for the sake of your Mission, that you are clever enough to survive the answer."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent Le Guin pastiche: an envoy (clearly Ekumen-flavored) slips away from protocol, observes a market that contradicts official briefings, is reprimanded, and faces a political Minister of Science in a test of wits. The structure follows the prompt faithfully and hits the ~1000 word target. Strengths: The market scene is the best part—the Grace woman mending a Lithic boy's collar, the cloth dyed with "gall-secretion of deep-trench sponges," the vendor's dialect and the "wolves sit on councils" line. The dialogue with Gray is genuinely sharp, particularly the "lock or key" exchange and Gray's cynical self-indictment about his ministry inventing "the reasons why the strong cage must lock the weak one." The prose has Le Guin's anthropological texture—subspecies divergence treated through economics, weaving, and respiration rather than spectacle. Weaknesses: The piece leans heavily on familiar Le Guin furniture (Ekumen, envoy, "species is a fiction") without adding much of its own. Some imagery strains—"ribs curving beneath tunics like the wicker frames of kites," "eyes small and dark like currants pressed into dough" (the dough/currant/almond-meal food similes cluster too densely around Gray). The pigment "containing no carbon, an organic compound" is a scientific howler. Vane's reprimand is efficient but generic—"attack of the liver" and "escaped steer" feel stock. The ending is a cliffhanger of the most predictable kind ("let us hope you survive the answer"), a thriller beat grafted onto an anthropological register, and it slightly betrays the Le Guin style, which would resist such melodrama. Solin's "trade follows the thread, not the bone" is a bit too neatly aphoristic for a young envoy under pressure. The subspecies worldbuilding is evocative but thin; the social structures are sketched rather than lived in. Still, the voice is consistent, the scene transitions clean, the dialogue mostly strong, and the central tension (official narrative vs. observed reality vs. Gray's darker counter-narrative) is genuinely layered. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 75.2
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The tiles beneath Vael’s boots had cracked during the third winter after the collapse, and life had not wasted the invitation. Sprouting from the fissured ceramic was a miniature forest of *Panellus stipticus*—glow-in-the-dark mushrooms, escaped runts from an aborted bioluminescent splicing run two years ago. They cast a bruised, ghostly cyan light across the basement lab, illuminating the rusted chrome of a broken autoclave and the condensate dripping down the walls. Vael blinked, his left eye twitching as the tapetum lucidum graft in his retina caught the fungal glow. It was a crude splice—chimeric feline DNA delivered via a bootleg adenovirus to stave off night-blindness when the district’s power grid finally surrendered. The upside was pristine low-light clarity; the downside was a persistent, fiery migraine whenever the sun rose, and a right tear duct that wept thin, milky bile every time he blinked. A fair trade. Most scavengers in the Outspan went blind before forty from cataracts caused by atmospheric particulate. At least Vael could still see down to the micron. He turned back to the workbench. His thermocycler—the holy grail of gene-splicing—was a monument to desperation. The chassis had once been an Italian espresso machine. Vael had stripped its boilers, hooked the copper coils to an Arduino motherboard salvaged from a child’s toy drone, and jury-rigged a cooling system out of two overclocked PC graphics-card fans and an aquarium pump. It was crude, but it held temperature. Denature at ninety-five Celsius. Anneal at fifty-six. Extend at seventy-two. *Clack-clack-hiss.* The machine rattled through a cycle, heating a rack of cut-down plastic Eppendorf tubes. Inside swam a cocktail of harvested *Thermus aquaticus* polymerase—brewed in a vat of fermenting compost out back—and the fraying genomic threads of a dead world. The door to the drainage tunnel groaned. Rust flaked, scattering like dried blood. "Vael?" A woman stepped through the vapor curtain, her silhouette framed by the fungal phosphorescence. It was Marrow, a fixer for the iron-mill settlements up the river. She wore three layers of patched ballistic nylon and carried a pressurized courier canister clipped to her chest rig. "You’re late," Vael said. His voice was hoarse, rattling in a chest altered by a homebrew pulmonary mod designed to filter sulfur smog. His ribs ached where the synthetic cartilage had grown too thick, a stiff cage that made deep breaths feel like swallowing needles. "Reagents don't stay cold forever, Marrow. My ice bath is melted ice-slush." "Patrols on the rail line," she said, unclipping the canister with calloused, grease-stained fingers. "They’re sweeping for un-chipped biomass. AgroCorp sentries are still active near the silos." "AgroCorp died twenty years ago." "Their automated drones didn't get the memo." Marrow set the canister on the stainless steel counter, avoiding the patches of creeping moss. "Here it is. Just like we agreed. Three hundred dried ampoules of clean diesel fuel, once the splice is confirmed." Vael unscrewed the canister’s pressure seal. A faint hiss of dry nitrogen puffed out, carrying a smell like parched earth. Inside lay a single, desiccated seed pod, resting in synthetic batting. It looked like an ordinary lentil, but its husk was stamped with a micro-laser serial number: *MON-HYB-8894*. "True-yield legume," Marrow whispered. "Nitrogen-fixing, high-protein, frost-hardy down to minus fifteen. If we plant this in the riverbed, the settlement eats through the winter." Vael picked it up with plastic-tipped tweezers. "You know what happened to the first batch they planted in the valley, don't you?" "Grew eight feet tall," Marrow replied. "Then went black and dissolved into slime before the pods opened." "Planned obsolescence," Vael said, his lip curling. "The grand design. AgroCorp didn't sell seeds; they leased biological software. Every generation had an embedded self-destruct: an apoptotic cascade coded to activate the moment the plant reached seed-bearing maturity in the second generation. If you didn't buy their proprietary suppressive spray each spring, your crop killed itself. When the company collapsed and the spray stopped shipping, the world starved." "Can you cut it out?" "Cut it? No. The kill-switch is woven through three different chromosomes," Vael said, setting the seed into a sterile ceramic mortar. "I can't edit it out cleanly with what I have here. But I can amplify the clean upstream sequences before the degradation markers kick in. Polymerase Chain Reaction. I tear the seed's cells apart, find the three fragments of un-corrupted DNA that govern the cold-hardiness and nitrogen absorption, and clone them a billion times over in the espresso machine. Then I stitch those amplicons into the backbone of a common, hardy river-weed." "Will it still taste like food?" "It’ll taste like boiled cardboard," Vael muttered, crushing the seed with a ceramic pestle until it was fine, pale dust. "But your people will stop burying their children in January." He worked with mechanical speed. His fingers, tipped with thickened, keratinized nails—another side effect of the graft therapies he took to prevent tissue rejection—didn't shake. He added lysis buffer to break open the cell membranes, spun the slurry in a centrifuge made from an angle-grinder mounted to a bucket, and drew off the clear supernatant containing the target nucleic acids. He added the primers he had synthesized weeks ago using degraded reagents and prayers, mixed in the nucleotides, and loaded the tubes into the rattling espresso machine. Vael keyed the Arduino. The PC fans screamed, a high-pitched whine that sent ripples across the damp condensation on the ceiling. *Cycle 1 of 35.* For two hours, they stood in silence, bathed in the cyan glow of the floor mushrooms. Vael sucked on a saline pouch to counteract the dry mouth his respiratory mods inflicted, his chest swelling stiffly, his feline eye reflecting the flickering readouts. Ninety-five degrees. Fifty-six. Seventy-two. Split the double helix. Bind the primers. Build the new strands. Double the DNA. Again. Again. Exponential resurrection. When the Arduino finally beeped its tinny, toy-like chime, Vael extracted the tiny vial. He pulled five microliters and loaded it into an agarose gel tray connected to a bank of car batteries. He didn't need UV light. He leaned in, his spliced eye widening, pupils dilating until the iris vanished. Through the translucent gel, the bands were visible to him as glowing, ultraviolet smudges. Three distinct, bright lines. Intact. Amplified. The corporate kill-switch, too large to be caught by his primers, had been left behind in the dregs. "We have viable yield," Vael breathed, the pain in his ribcage fading behind a surge of cold adrenaline. "The amplified genome is clean." Marrow exhaled a breath she seemed to have held for years. She reached into her rucksack and set a heavy, dented metal crate onto the table. The smell of high-grade diesel hit the air, sharp and chemically sweet. "Contract fulfilled," she said. Vael sealed the amplified DNA in a cold-pack, handing it to her like a holy relic. "Keep it out of the light until you splice it into the rootstock. And Marrow?" She paused at the tunnel entrance, looking back into the glowing, subterranean rot. "Don't tell them where it came from," Vael said, watching his own green-glowing knuckles pulse against the counter. "I don't think AgroCorp would like what I’ve done with their property."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, atmospheric biopunk chapter that hits nearly all prompt requirements: post-apocalyptic setting with corporate planned genetic obsolescence, jury-rigged lab equipment (espresso machine thermocycler, angle-grinder centrifuge, toy-drone Arduino), physical toll and upsides of self-modification (feline tapetum graft, pulmonary mods), and a black market contract as the plot spine. The prose is confident and technically flavored, with strong sensory details (glow mushrooms, condensation, diesel smell). The worldbuilding exposition about AgroCorp's kill-switch is delivered efficiently through dialogue, though it leans toward lecture-like "as you know" exchanges. The science is hand-wavy but plausible-sounding enough for the genre. Weaknesses: Marrow is thin as a character, existing mainly to deliver exposition and payment; the plot resolves without complication, making the contract feel low-stakes and frictionless; some phrasing strains ("exponential resurrection," "watching his own green-glowing knuckles pulse" — a late, unexplained detail implying his mods glow, slightly incongruent). The ending line is stylish but the "AgroCorp would like" quip is a familiar beat. Dialogue is serviceable but occasionally expository. Overall: polished genre fiction, engaging but not transcendent. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel’s air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone, a dry, metallic vibration that Arthur Neegan felt through the soles of his vulcanized boots. It was the sound of recycled oxygen and thin Martian economics, but the ship itself belonged to neither the Combine nor the local Mining Guild. Arthur looked down at his calloused fingers. A week ago, those hands had been adjusting thermal drills in the red dust of the Cimmeria basin, coaxing low-yield silicates from stubborn ground to satisfy a company debt that never seemed to diminish. Then the core drill had struck the anomaly: a dark, dense vein of Azra, radiating a mild, prickling warmth that caused his handheld dosimeters to chatter like frantic cicadas. Within forty-eight hours, the silence of his isolated claim had been shattered. Four men had arrived in an unflagged skimmer, their charcoal-grey tunics bearing the modest, gold-threaded needle of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. They had carried sidearms holstered with bureaucratic casualness and carried an invitation delivered in tones that made refusal an exercise in suicide. Now, the drone shifted frequency. The attitude thrusters fired with a muted, hydraulic thump. "Docking sequence initiated," an artificial voice clipped over the cabin speaker. "Station *Geryon*, low orbital apogee." The hatch hissed open, revealing an escort whose polished brass buttons gleamed under harsh fluorescent tubes. Arthur stood up, adjusting his coarse flannel collar. He was a creature of gravity and rock; the magnetic pull of the orbital deck felt unnaturally light, making his stride awkward. He was led down a series of stark, pressurized corridors lined with heavy copper-mesh conduits—shielding against the fierce radiation belts, or perhaps against something manufactured inside. At the end of the central spine, a heavy pneumatic door slid back into the bulkhead, revealing an observation lounge. The room was unexpectedly quiet. A curved pane of thick quartz looked out upon the vast, ochre curvature of Mars. Against that backdrop of rust and dry canyons stood a thin, ascetic man in a high-collared civilian coat, sipping from a glass bulb of amber bulb-wine. Beside him, an obsolete vacuum-tube computer bank ticked methodically, punching telemetry data onto narrow paper strips. "Mr. Neegan," the man said, turning. His features were sharp, pale, and entirely devoid of Martian windburn. "Please, sit. The gravity generator is calibrated to Earth-standard, I'm afraid. An old man's vanity." Arthur sat in the low leather chair opposite the desk. "You're not from the Antares Consulate on Earth. And you’re certainly not Martian administration." "A keen deduction, though hardly difficult," the man replied with a dry, pleasant smile. "I am High Commissioner Vane. Technically, I represent the Trade Council of the Outer Periphery. Practically, I represent survival. Yours, mine, and perhaps that of several billion people who do not yet realize their stoves are about to be lit with nuclear fire." Arthur leaned back, folding his arms. "I'm a mining engineer, Commissioner. If you wanted to confiscate my claim, you could have bribed the District Recorder in Noctis Labyrinthus for fifty credits. You didn't need a shielded orbital cruiser." Vane chuckled, a sound like dry leaves. "The District Recorder? My dear Arthur, if the Recorder saw the spectroscopic analysis of your claim, he would have been shot by his own deputies within an hour. You misunderstand what you have under your boots." Vane pressed a stud on the console. A three-dimensional hololith flickered into being between them—a lattice of atomic structures, glowing an eerie, pulsing violet. "Azra," Vane said softly. "The Terrestrial Combine believes it to be merely an efficient catalytic isotope—a clever way to cut fuel costs on the lunar run. Even the Martian Syndicates think it is simply a leverage tool, an economic bludgeon to break their debt-slavery. They are all thinking like merchants with ledgers." Vane leaned forward, the smile fading. "Three grams of Azra, introduced into a standard thorium reactor, accelerates decay by a factor of eight hundred. It reduces a century’s worth of containment into a instantaneous microsecond burst. Harness it in a magnetic constriction field, and you have an interstellar drive that makes the Antares run a matter of weeks rather than decades. Remove the field..." "You have a planet-buster," Arthur finished, the dry air suddenly cold in his throat. "You have the total collapse of the Balance of Power," Vane corrected precisely. "Earth has the population. Mars has the raw ores. The Outer Worlds have the industrial shipyards. For fifty years, peace has been preserved because none of us could reach the other before mutual annihilation took its toll. Your vein contains enough unrefined Azra to fuel three battle-fleets—or vaporize the Martian ice caps." "And you want the deed," Arthur said. "I am offering you an escape from history, Mr. Neegan. The Combine has already dispatched a division of security frigates; they will arrive in sixteen days. If you are still on Mars, you will suffer a fatal operational accident in your own airlock, and your claim will revert to the state. If you sell to the Martian rebels, they will mismanage the extraction, irradiate the Tharsis plateau, and provoke a planetary blockade." Vane slid an unadorned dataslate across the desk. It bore an authorization seal, blank except for a cryptographic key. "Sign the conveyance to the Antares Trust. In return: three million credits, converted into anonymous Outer Colony bearer bonds. A stateroom on the *Hyperion*, departing tonight for the Jovian neutral zones. A new name. A quiet life." Arthur looked down at the slate, then out the window at the red planet below. He thought of the indentured men in the barracks of Cimmeria, coughing red dust into grey filters, living on rations borrowed against wages they would never see. "And the Azra?" Arthur asked. "What does Antares do with it?" Vane stood, smoothing his coat. "We secure it, Mr. Neegan. In a vault so deep that not even the Combine’s deep-radar can find it. We maintain the peace." Arthur looked up, his engineer's mind running the logic. "Or you hold the knife to everyone's throat. If you had the fleet to protect the claim, you wouldn't need my signature to maintain the legal pretense against the Combine. You're bluffing, Commissioner. You don't have the strength to take the claim by force—not yet." Vane’s eyes narrowed, the warmth vanishing entirely, replaced by the cold, vacant stare of deep space. "A brilliant deduction, Arthur," Vane whispered. "Now consider the corollary: if I cannot take the claim by force, how far will I go to ensure Earth never touches it either?"
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece opens aboard the transfer vessel as instructed, delivers a dialogue-heavy meeting with an unknown party (Vane), and sows intrigue effectively. The Asimovian flavor is present: vacuum-tube computers, balance-of-power geopolitics, dialogue-driven exposition of a scientific concept (Azra's decay acceleration), and a chess-like negotiation ending in a threat. The prose is clean and controlled, with some vivid touches (dosimeters chattering like cicadas, "dry leaves" chuckle). Arthur's deduction that Vane is bluffing gives him agency and intelligence, and the ending line lands as a genuine menace. Weaknesses: some typos/awkwardness ("an instantaneous microsecond burst," "amber bulb-wine"), and the worldbuilding occasionally tips into exposition-dump territory—Vane explains too much too neatly, a common Asimov pastiche issue. The plot beats (mysterious invitation, offer, refusal, veiled threat) are somewhat predictable in their arc, though well executed. Characters are functional rather than deeply nuanced; Vane is a familiar "cold commissioner" type. Still, the piece fulfills the prompt's requirements faithfully and reads as competent, professional genre fiction. Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smelled of its usual vinegar and iron—acetic stop bath and fixer that clung to the weave of my leather jacket like bad perfume. Under the amber-red glow of the safelights, the world lost its color and settled into shades of blood and ink. Elliot was leaning over the developing tray, rocking it with two fingers. His nails were chipped with black lacquer, rings made of bent silver spoons catching the dim light. At nineteen, he dressed like a Victorian ghost haunting an underground rave: moth-eaten charcoal knitwear, raw-hemmed skirts over distressed denim, and a shock of raven hair that fell over dark, wide-set eyes. I was twenty-five, with a buzzcut and a reputation in the department for being the woman who told you precisely how to fix your exposure and whose bed you were allowed into if you kept up. I liked hard lines, clear directions, and partners who knew their scripts. But for three months, watching Elliot quietly build layered, haunting double-exposures had unspooled something tightly wound in my chest. "The shadows are blowing out again," he murmured. His voice was naturally low, but it had a feathered edge, like chalk on slate. "You’re leaving it in the developer ten seconds too long," I said, moving behind him. My instinct was to put a hand over his wrist to stop the tray, to take the tongs and steer. I did that with everyone. But standing near Elliot, I felt an unfamiliar hitch in my throat. I didn't want to muscle him out of the frame. I just stood there, breathing in the scent of clove cigarettes and clean cotton coming off his collar. "Dani?" he asked, not looking up from the ghostly grey image emerging under the surface of the chemical bath. "Yeah?" "Can I… tell you something weird?" "I’m an experimental printmaker, Elliot. Weird is our baseline." He lifted the print with bamboo tongs, letting the liquid sheet off into the tray. His shoulders were tense, pulled up toward his earrings. "I've been thinking about what you said last week. About the portraits I took of myself. How you said the subject looked like they were waiting for permission to exist." "I was being an arrogant critic," I deflected softly, surprised by the sudden fragility in the room. "No. You were right." He transferred the print into the stop bath. The liquid swished rhythmically. "I’ve been… trying things on. Not just clothes. Pronouns. The idea that maybe 'he' is just a jacket I forgot to take off." He paused, his throat bobbing as he swallowed. "I think I’m somewhere in between. Or maybe on the other side entirely. I haven’t said it out loud to anyone. But you look at people like you can see the grain beneath the surface. I figured… I don't know." The words hung in the red air, delicate as blown glass. A jolt ran through me—half electrifying thrill, half sudden disorientation. I’d spent my whole dating life gravitating toward sharply defined archetypes: leather-jacketed guys with broad shoulders or butch women with razor-cut jaws. Masculinity and femininity were cards I knew how to play against. But Elliot was standing in the middle of a shifting horizon, handing me the map to a place he hadn’t even charted yet. My immediate impulse—my muscle memory—was to seize control. *Tell me what you need, let me protect you, let me take you shopping, let me drive.* It was the easy role: the older, confident dyke guiding the younger kid through the dark. Except it wasn't just protective. I wanted to cup the curve of his soft jaw in my palm. I wanted to unbutton that frayed cardigan and find out what made him shiver. And admitting that to myself made my stomach swoop with vertigo. Was I queer enough for this? Selfish for wanting him while he was in pieces? "Elliot," I started, stepping closer. "That’s—" I moved too fast. My hip caught the edge of the dry bench, knocking against the open cardboard box of fresh Ilford multi-grade photo paper we’d set out to reload the negative carriers. "Wait—" Elliot gasped, turning instinctively. In my scramble to catch the sliding box, my forearm brushed the master toggle on the wall—the white fluorescent overheads. A harsh, blinding brilliance tore through the room. The darkroom vanished, replaced by sterile, buzzing white tubes. For three devastating seconds, we froze like animals caught in high beams. My eyes burned. The lid of the paper box was off; twenty-five pristine sheets of silver gelatin paper lay naked under the full blast of the ceiling lights, instantly ruined, their sensitive chemical emulsion drinking in the glare until they were dead. "Fuck!" I slammed the toggle down. The red glow returned, but our pupils took long, agonized seconds to adjust. Darkness rushed back in, thick and suffocating. We stood in silence, chests heaving. Fifty dollars of paper, entirely wiped out. Then, Elliot let out a breath that cracked into a laugh. "Well," he whispered, leaning his forehead against the wooden rim of the enlarger station. "There goes the contrast study." I blinked through the purple afterimages dancing behind my eyelids. "I completely blew it. God, Elliot, I'm sorry. I was trying to... I don't know what I was doing." "It's just paper," he said. He didn't sound angry; he sounded loose, the paralyzing tension broken by the sheer absurdity of the disaster. He turned around, leaning his lower back against the bench, looking up at me through his fringe. In the ruby-tinted gloom, the soft curve of his cheekbones and the delicate hollow of his neck were impossibly beautiful. "I was trying to take charge," I admitted, my voice dropping lower than usual, stripped of its swagger. "Like I always do. But this isn't my project, Elliot. Your life, I mean. It’s yours." "I didn't tell you so you could fix it," Elliot said softly, meeting my gaze with a steady, quiet courage that made my breath hitch. "I told you because when you look at me, you don't treat me like a mistake. Even when I feel like one." The distance between us felt magnetized. My usual script—the aggressive flirtation, the playful commands—evaporated, leaving something raw and terrifyingly new. "Can I touch you?" I asked, the question feeling strange and heavy on my tongue. Giving away the reins was not my style, but seeing the faint flush rise on his cheeks made my pulse hammer. "Yes," he whispered. I reached out, abandoning my usual firmness, and gently brushed a strand of dark hair behind his ear. My thumb grazed his earlobe, then trailed along the soft line of his jaw. He leaned into the touch, a tiny, shuddering sigh escaping his lips. "Whatever you are," I said, the words settling the riot in my own chest, "it looks good on you." Elliot smiled, small and brilliant in the amber dark, and reached out to catch my hand, lacing his silver-ringed fingers through mine.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of creative writing that fulfills the prompt's requirements with notable skill. The darkroom setting is used effectively, with the red safelight creating the requested confessional atmosphere, and the technical photography details (developer, stop bath, fixer, Ilford paper) ground the scene in authenticity. The characterization of Dani is well-executed: her assertive, take-charge persona is established efficiently through concrete details ("the woman who told you precisely how to fix your exposure and whose bed you were allowed into if you kept up"), and her internal conflict—wanting to seize control versus giving Elliot agency—is dramatized rather than merely stated. The ruined paper incident is a clever device: it literalizes Dani's clumsiness in this unfamiliar emotional territory, breaks the tension naturally, and earns the shift toward vulnerability. Elliot's gender questioning is handled with sensitivity, and his line about "he" being "just a jacket I forgot to take off" is a genuinely good image. The prose is polished, with strong sensory work (vinegar and iron, clove cigarettes, silver spoon rings). Occasionally it tips toward the ornate—"delicate as blown glass," "shifting horizon, handing me the map to a place he hadn't even charted yet"—but it stays within the bounds of the narrator's arty, self-aware voice rather than becoming purple. The dialogue is naturalistic and does real work, particularly Elliot's "I told you because when you look at me, you don't treat me like a mistake." Minor criticisms: the physical comedy of the light switch feels slightly convenient as a plot mechanism, though it's plausible. Dani's internal monologue occasionally over-explains her feelings ("Was I queer enough for this? Selfish for wanting him while he was in pieces?")—a touch of telling in an otherwise show-heavy piece. The ending is warm but earned, since the piece has done the work of establishing both characters' vulnerability. The word count is roughly on target. The resolution arrives a bit quickly and neatly, but the piece is a single scene, so this is forgivable. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 55.7
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The midday sun struck the travertine stone of the Trevi Fountain with blinding intensity, but Ben Montgomery saw none of it. He was entirely consumed by page 142 of his battered, navy-bound architectural guide, tracing a footnote on Salvi’s Corinthian pilasters while stepping blindly backward off the curb. Tires shrieked, rubber smoking against basalt cobblestones. Ben yelped, leaping back as a matte-black Moto Guzzi skidded sideways, stopping precisely two inches from his shins. The engine purred like an agitated leopard. “*Ma sei totalmente cieco, o hai deciso di morire oggi?!*” The rider tore off a scuffed helmet, releasing an unruly cascade of espresso-dark curls. Amber eyes glared up at him from a face of sharp, aristocratic angles smeared with a streak of road grease. She looked barely thirty, dressed in an oil-stained leather jacket and steel-toed boots. Ben stood paralyzed, clutching his book to his chest like a shield. “I—*mi dispiace tanto!* Oh God, *scusi*, signorina. I was engrossed in Salvi’s masonry, which is obviously no excuse for spatial incompetence—” The fury in the woman’s eyes dissolved into startled incredulity. “English,” she said in crisp, venomous Italian, before switching to heavily accented, melodic English. “Of course. A professor with his nose in paper, walking into Roman traffic. You nearly dented my tank.” Ben looked down. Across the sculpted flank of the fuel tank ran a violent, brilliant slash of canary-yellow paint over crumpled metal. “Did I… did I do that?” She snorted, a wicked half-smile curving her lips. “No. That was a fruit vendor’s cart in Trastevere last Tuesday. He wouldn’t move his melons. But you almost gave it a twin.” She assessed him: wrinkled linen shirt, wire-rimmed glasses askew, pale skin blushing a furious crimson. A slow, predatory glint appeared in her eye. “You’re shaking, Professor.” “Ben,” he stammered. “Dr. Benjamin Montgomery. And I assure you, my adrenaline is simply—” “Alessandra,” she interrupted, kicking down the passenger pegs with the heel of her boot. She slapped the pillion seat. “Get on.” “I beg your pardon?” “I have two courier manifests to deliver to the Piazza Navona, and you look like you’re about to faint into the Trevi basin. Plus, you need an education that doesn’t smell like moldy library paste. *Andiamo.*” *** Twenty minutes later, Ben had abandoned all dignity. His fingers were white-knuckled around Alessandra’s leather waist, his chest pressed firmly against the warm, vibrating curve of her back as she carved through Roman gridlock like a scalpel. She treated red lights as mild suggestions and pedestrian zones as private speedways. Every near-miss with a bus drew a joyful bark of laughter from her, vibrating directly through her spine into Ben’s ribs. He was terrified. He was entirely, intoxicatingly alive. When she cut the engine in an alleyway choked with laundry lines near the Campo de' Fiori, Ben’s legs were so gelatinous he nearly tripped dismounting. “Stay,” she ordered, disappearing into a high-end leather artisan’s workshop to drop off a parcel. She emerged two minutes later, swinging an espresso cup she’d somehow acquired, followed closely by the artisan himself, who shouted pleasantries after her. As they walked toward a café, Alessandra bumped lightly against Ben’s side. With a deft, magician’s flick of her wrist, she spun a small, glittering object between her fingers: a heavy, sterling-silver monogrammed thimble from the shop. Ben halted. “Alessandra. Is that…?” She slipped it into her breast pocket without missing a beat, turning with wide, impossibly innocent eyes. “Is what, *Dottore*?” “You just stole that.” “Stole is an ugly, Protestant word,” she murmured, stepping close enough that Ben caught the scent of her skin—bergamot, gasoline, and summer rain. “I liberated it. The artisan has fifty. And it looked lonely.” “That’s illegal,” Ben whispered, but his voice lacked any academic authority. It cracked, betrayed by the sudden proximity of her parted lips. “Then call the Carabinieri,” she whispered back, eyes dancing with challenge. “Tell them the bad courier woman took you hostage.” Ben swallowed hard, his gaze dipping involuntarily to her collarbone. “I… I wouldn't want to waste their time.” Alessandra’s laugh was low, rich, and smug. She grabbed him by the lapels of his rumpled blazer and pulled him toward the smell of roasting beans. *** By dusk, Ben had eaten *supplì* that scalded the roof of his mouth on the curb of an empty palazzo, listened to Alessandra insult an overbearing taxi driver with poetry-level vulgarity, and watched her surreptitiously pocket a porcelain salt shaker from an upscale trattoria just because she liked the cobalt glaze. He hadn't opened his guidebook once. Now, they stood on the forbidden upper balustrade of the Janiculum Hill. Alessandra had bypassed the rusted padlock of a municipal utility gate using a hair-pin and sheer, stubborn audacity. Rome lay below them, drowned in bruised violet and molten gold. The bells of a dozen bell towers tolled the vespers, their chimes floating up through the pine trees. “You’re quiet,” she said softly, leaning her elbows against the chipped stone. For the first time all day, the frantic dynamo inside her seemed to idle. “I was just thinking,” Ben said, looking at the city, then at the sharp silhouette of her profile against the dusk, “that my sabbatical itinerary said I should have spent today cataloging the epigraphy in the Capitoline.” “Sounds boring.” “It would have been entirely safe,” Ben agreed, turning toward her. “Predictable. Monastic.” “And instead?” “Instead, I’ve been an accessory to at least two petty larcenies and three dozen moving violations.” Alessandra turned to face him, the fading amber light catching the mischievous warmth in her eyes. “Regrets, Professor?” “Not a single one,” Ben said quietly, his voice surprisingly steady. The flirtatious banter dissolved, replaced by a sudden, heavy gravity. The evening breeze pushed a strand of dark hair across her cheek; without thinking, Ben reached out and tucked it behind her ear. His fingers brushed the warm shell of her skin, and she didn't pull away. Her breath hitched—just once, subtle enough that a less observant man would have missed it. Alessandra closed the distance between them, stepping into his space until the worn leather of her jacket brushed his chest. She reached up, wrapping her fingers around the nape of his neck, and pulled him down into a kiss that tasted of bitter espresso and sweet rebellion. It was neither polite nor scholarly. Ben met it desperately, his hands finding the curve of her waist, anchoring himself to the hurricane. When she broke away, breathless, she tapped his chest with a single knuckle, her enigmatic grin firmly back in place. “Good,” she murmured. “Now check your coat.” Ben blinked, disoriented, reaching into his blazer pocket. His fingers closed around cold, heavy metal: the silver thimble, wrapped neatly in a torn receipt. Beneath it, scrawled in black marker, was a phone number and four words in Italian: *Tomorrow. Don't be late.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, polished piece that fulfills the brief with notable efficiency. The opening collision at the Trevi Fountain is well-staged, with the near-miss rendered in crisp physical detail (the skidding Moto Guzzi, the dented yellow tank). The character voices are distinct from the first exchange: Ben's fussy, footnote-laden fluster ("engrossed in Salvi's masonry, which is obviously no excuse for spatial incompetence") contrasts effectively with Alessandra's rapid, imperious wit. The Italian is deployed naturally rather than as ornament. The kleptomania brief is handled well — the thimble theft is shown through action, and Alessandra's justification ("Stole is an ugly, Protestant word... I liberated it") is the strongest line in the piece, characterful and funny without over-exaining. The salt shaker later reinforces the habit subtly, as requested. The escalation structure (motorcycle ride, thefts, breaking into the Janiculum) tracks Ben's gradual willingness convincingly; his "accessory to at least two petty larcenies and three dozen moving violations" line lands as a well-earned summary of his quiet rebellion. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally tips into stock romantic phrasing — "tasted of bitter espresso and sweet rebellion," "anchoring himself to the hurricane," "espresso-dark curls" — competent but familiar. The kiss scene is the most conventional beat, relying on gestures (tucking hair behind ear, breath hitching) that are genre boilerplate. Alessandra's enigmatic quality is asserted more than deeply explored; her sudden stillness at dusk is a nice touch but her interiority remains thin, which is arguably intentional but limits emotional complexity. The ending (the returned thimble with phone number) is a satisfying, clever payoff that avoids saccharine resolution, though "Tomorrow. Don't be late" is a slightly predictable final flourish. The scene-break structure suits the "interconnected short scenes" instruction, pacing is tight, and nothing meanders. Dialogue is generally sharp, though Alessandra occasionally verges on quirk-dispenser. Overall this is skilled, professional commercial fiction — engaging and well-crafted, if not formally inventive.
