+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 77.0
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon sign over the register flickers with a low, rhythmic buzz that usually drives me crazy by midnight, but tonight it’s almost soothing. The Last Outpost is running at its usual lazy, low-gravity hum. Outside the reinforced viewport, the jagged iron chunks of the Veil Belt drift through the Andromeda dark like sleepy leviathans. Inside, it smells of charred kelp cakes, stale cooling fluid, and the yeast-heavy steam of my homemade barley draft. “I’m telling you, Nets, the man has the emotional range of a rusted servo,” Corin says, resting three of her four furry chins on her primary set of hands. “He’s a deep-core driller, Corin,” I say, sliding a polished glass under the tap. “You knew that when you agreed to split an oxygen lease with him. Drillers don’t talk about their feelings. They express intimacy through preventative atmospheric maintenance.” “He bought me a valve wrench for our anniversary.” “An antique brass valve wrench,” I point out, setting a fresh mug of amber foam in front of her. “That’s practically a sonnet in Belt-dialect.” She huffs, but a small smile parts her whiskers. “You always make excuses for the hopeless ones.” “Takes one to know one. Just ask him if he wants to split a ration pack on the observation deck tomorrow. If he says no, the next round is on the house.” “Deal.” Across the floor, near the sabacc tables, a sharp *smash* cuts through the low drone of conversation. A glass accidentally shatters against the grated deck, followed by an embarrassed yelp from young Dax, our newest busboy. “Don’t toss the pieces down the waste chute, Dax!” I call out, leaning over the zinc counter. “Recycle bin three! If the intake clogs again, you’re the one crawling into the compactor!” “Sorry, Nets! Got it!” Dax squeaks, already scrambling with a mag-broom. I shake my head, rubbing the knot of tension at the base of my neck. My past life—the one with corporate dossiers, high-stakes security clearance, and people trying to put clean energy-burn holes through my ribcage—never had messes this simple. I’m entirely too soft on these kids, and my accounting is a shambles, but my hands are steady and nobody asks why my papers only go back seven cycles. In a place this far out, equilibrium is everything. The hydraulic hiss of the airlock door breathes a gust of recycled, chilled air into the room. Footsteps follow—erratic, stumbling, too fast for a miner coming off an eighteen-hour rock-clearing shift. The newcomer slides onto a stool at the far, shadowed corner of the bar. He’s an Elusian, though in the worst shape I’ve ever seen one: his skin is a mottled, stress-pale lilac, his traveling cloak is singed along the hem, and his tentacled dreads are completely askew, writhing in frantic, involuntary micro-spasms against his neck. He drops both trembling hands flat on the scarred copper counter. “Vega whisky, neat,” he breathes, his voice scraping like gravel in an air duct. “Better make that a double.” I don’t move immediately. Vega whisky is thirty credits an ounce, smells like peat smoke and ionized copper, and is ninety-two percent proof. It’s not a drinking drink; it’s an anesthetic. “Coming up,” I say quietly. I pull the heavy, square-cut bottle from the bottom shelf, pop the seal, and pour two generous fingers into a lowball tumbler. I slide it across the zinc. He snatches it, his fingers slick with cold sweat, and downs half the glass in one searing gulp. He gasps, his bioluminescent skin flashing a sharp, defensive cyan before dulling back to ash. “Rough run through the rocks?” I ask, keeping my voice gentle, the way you speak to a jumpy rescue hound. “Rocks don’t shoot back,” he mutters, staring into the remaining amber liquid. I pause, rag in hand. “The Belt’s neutral territory. Even the syndicates keep their guns cold within ten clicks of the Outpost.” “Wasn't syndicates.” He glances over his shoulder toward the heavy, vacuum-rated blast doors, his tentacles twitching violently. “You’re Nettle, right? Nets?” “Depends on who’s asking. Port Authority usually hears my name is Brenda.” “The surveyor at Dock Four said you were the one to talk to. Said you used to run high-band comms for... well. Before you settled out here.” My stomach tightens, an old, cold reflex. I keep my rag moving in slow, rhythmic circles on the bar top. “I pour drinks, friend. Sometimes I unjam the ice maker. That’s the full extent of my technical portfolio.” “Don’t give me the backwater barkeep act,” he whispers, leaning in. He smells of scorched plasteel and stale adrenaline. “I don’t have time for it. Neither do you.” “Look, mister—” “Tarek,” he cuts in. “My name is Tarek. I was running salvage along the Outer Ridge. Sub-sector Nine. Past the warning buoys.” “Nothing out in Nine except empty void and debris from the First Expansion,” I say, keeping my tone light, though my grip on the rag tightens. “Dead space.” “It’s not dead.” Tarek reaches into the folds of his scorched cloak and sets something on the counter between us. It’s a data core, roughly the size of a plum, but it isn’t standard issue. It’s seamless, matte black, and constructed from an alloy that seems to drink the tavern’s ambient neon light without reflecting a photon. More importantly, pulsing beneath its obsidian shell is a faint, rhythmic crimson glow. A military-grade transponder, broadcasting on a frequency I haven't seen since I burned my real identity and fled the Core worlds. “Found it lodged in the hull of a derelict freighter,” Tarek says, his voice dropping so low I have to lean across the bar to hear him over the murmur of the patrons. “The ship was stripped clean. No bodies. No cargo. Just this, wired directly into their main reactor, burning through the reserve cells.” “Then why bring it here?” I ask, my pulse suddenly loud in my ears. “You should have dumped it in the nearest sun.” “I tried to scrub the signature, but I tripped a hard-locked fail-safe,” he says, his eyes wide, pupils completely blown out. “It pinged out a tight-beam transmission forty minutes ago. Deep space. Toward the rim.” Before I can answer, the outpost’s primary atmospheric lights flicker once, twice, dipping into amber emergency low-power before struggling back up. High above us, deep within the rock-anchored chassis of the station, the long-range proximity buoy emits a single, muffled, mournful chime. Tarek looks up at the ceiling, his tentacles flattening tight against his skull. “They aren’t miners, Nets,” he whispers. “And they didn't come to dock.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, well-executed cozy sci-fi chapter that hits nearly all of the prompt's requirements. The first-person present-tense voice is maintained consistently, the setting (The Last Outpost, asteroid belt bar) is established with sensory efficiency, and the chapter opens with the right "lazy hum" before the stranger arrives to introduce conflict. Dialogue percentage is roughly at the requested 60%, and the conflict (the mysterious data core, the tripped fail-safe, the approaching unknown ship) is clearly established and left unresolved, as instructed. Strengths: The banter with Corin about the valve-wrench anniversary is charming and does double duty — establishing tone and Nets' character as a soft-hearted fixer. The worldbuilding details (Belt-dialect, oxygen leases, Elusian bioluminescent skin, "preventative atmospheric maintenance" as driller intimacy) feel organic rather than infodumped. The data core description — an alloy that "drinks" the neon light — is a genuinely evocative image. The ending line, "They aren't miners, Nets... And they didn't come to dock," is a strong chapter-ending hook. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally leans on stock thriller phrasing — "my pulse suddenly loud in my ears," "an old, cold reflex," "eyes wide, pupils completely blown out." The Elusian stranger is functionally a plot-delivery device; his characterization is all distress signals and no personality. Some of Nets' backstory hints ("people trying to put clean energy-burn holes through my ribcage") are a touch overwrought. The "rocks don't shoot back" exchange is effective but familiar. The piece is genre-comfortable rather than surprising — it executes the cozy-scifi-with-arriving-trouble template faithfully, without subverting or refreshing it. Still, the execution is professional, coherent, and engaging throughout, with no structural or logical missteps. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The trucker who hauled me across the state line told me to get the fuck out somewhere near the edge of the French Quarter. His parting gift was a lecture on how girls from the holler who chop off their hair and ask to be called *he* or *they* end up face-down in a swamp. I slammed his passenger door hard enough to rattle the side mirror, but the second his taillights dissolved into the morning smog, my knees shook so violently I had to lean against a brick wall that smelled like stale beer and river rot. Forty-eight hours ago, I was eating frozen waffles in a kitchen with peeling laminate, trying to find the guts to explain that the daughter they thought they raised never actually existed. Mom didn't yell. That was the worst part. She just looked at me like I was a carton of milk that had turned sour in the fridge—something to be thrown out with the Tuesday trash. Step-dad called me an abomination before going back to his ESPN alerts. By midnight, I had four hundred bucks swiped from the emergency jar behind the flour canister, three binders crammed into a beat-up Jansport, and a one-way ticket to Anywhere Else. Now, it’s 2:00 PM, and New Orleans is melting my cheap sneakers to the sidewalk. A street musician's saxophone plays in the background as I walk down the crowded corridor of Royal Street. It isn’t the smooth, polished elevator jazz they play in dentists' offices back in Pigeon Forge; it's raspy, erratic, screaming over the chattering tourists and the clatter of horse carriages. It throbs right behind my temples. Every beat feels like a warning: *You don't belong here. You're sixteen. You have nowhere to sleep.* "You stare any harder at that psychic's window, kid, your eyes are gonna crack the glass." The voice comes from a doorway between an antique shop and a voodoo tourist trap. I freeze, instinctively pulling my elbows in, defensive posture dialed to eleven. Sitting on an overturned milk crate is a kid who looks maybe a year older than me. Dirty denim vest, no shirt underneath, arms covered in scratchy stick-and-poke tattoos of constellations and dagger blades. A faded baseball cap is pulled low over a mess of tangled dark curls. "I'm not staring," I lie, my voice coming out thinner than I want it to. "And I'm not a kid." "Sure you aren't." They snort, tossing an unlit cigarette from one hand to the other. "And I'm the Queen of England. You got runaway stamped on your forehead in neon pink, Tennessee." My stomach drops into my gut. "How do you—" "The orange mud still caked on your Vans, for one. And you walk like you think the sidewalks are rigged with landmines." The kid stands up. They’re shorter than I thought, lean as a stray dog, with sharp collarbones and a dark purple bruise blossoming along the edge of their jawline. They extend a hand with grime beneath the nails. "Cricket. Pronouns are they/them, before you hurt yourself trying to guess." The relief that hits me is so sudden and pathetic it almost brings tears to my eyes, but I swallow it down. I can’t afford to be soft. Soft gets you put in the back of a squad car or worse. "Taylor," I say, shaking their hand. Their grip is surprisingly calloused and cold. "They/them too." Cricket’s mouth twitches into something that might be a smile if it didn't look so exhausted. "Well, Taylor-They-Them, you picked a weird-ass week to defect to the swamp. You eaten?" "Not since yesterday." Cricket tilts their head toward the street. "Walk with me. Jackson Square's got bread if you know which cart workers hate their bosses enough to drop a box." I shouldn't follow them. Every lecture from every assembly I ever zoned out of screams that following a stranger into an alley is how you end up a statistic. But my ribs ache from my binder, my mouth tastes like dust, and the loneliness pressing down on my chest feels heavier than the Louisiana humidity. So I fall into step beside them. The saxophone music trails behind us, sliding into a low, mournful blue note before the roar of traffic swallows it. "So," Cricket says, dodging a pair of sunburned tourists with giant plastic cups of daiquiris. "What was the final straw? Piss-poor foster home, or holy-roller parents?" "Holy-rollers," I mutter, looking down. "Came out. They treated me like a biohazard." "Classic." Cricket kicks an empty plastic bottle into the gutter. "Mine were the kind who liked their discipline with a closed fist and a belt buckle. Left Atlanta three months ago. Been drifting along the coast ever since." There is something jittery about Cricket, though. As we turn onto a quieter cross-street lined with crumbling balconies and heavy iron ferns, they keep looking back over their shoulder. Not like they’re checking for cops—something more specific. Their hand stays clamped tight over the strap of a heavy leather duffel slung across their chest. "What's in the bag?" I ask before I can stop myself. Cricket stops dead. Their eyes, wide and hyper-alert, snap to mine. For a second, the street kid swagger completely vanishes, replaced by a raw, terrifying panic. "Stuff that isn't mine," Cricket whispers, their voice dropping an octave. "And if anyone asks if you've seen a guy named Marcus with a scar through his left eyebrow, you run. You don't talk, you don't look him in the eye. You just haul ass." My heart begins hammering an erratic rhythm against my ribs. *God, I am so stupid.* I traded the suffocating misery of Tennessee for a back-alley setup. I take half a step backward, calculating the distance back to the crowded boulevard where the saxophone was still whining in the distance. Cricket catches the terror in my expression and sighs, their shoulders slumping. The hard edges crumble just a fraction, revealing someone just as terrified, just as bruised, just as completely out of options as I am. "Look," Cricket says quietly, wiping sweat from their forehead. "I'm not gonna drag you into my shit. We'll get some day-old po'boys from a buddy of mine by the river, and then you can take off if you want. But out here? Being alone is how you get eaten alive, Taylor. You need to learn the ropes before nightfall, or the Quarter will chew you up and spit you in the Mississippi." I look at Cricket—at the bruise on their jaw, the trembling fingers, the defiant tilt of their chin that mirrors the face I made in my bathroom mirror two nights ago right before I packed my life into a backpack. Two days ago, I destroyed my life so I could finally start living it. Nobody said the living part was going to be safe. "Lead the way," I say, hitching my backpack higher on my shoulders. "I'm starving."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong YA chapter that fulfills the brief efficiently. Taylor's voice is consistent: sardonic, anxious, self-aware, with a convincing Tennessee-to-New Orleans displacement. The opening trucker detail, the sour-milk coming-out memory, and the binder ache ground the character physically and emotionally. Cricket is a well-drawn foil—streetwise, guarded, with a duffel-bag mystery and a Marcus threat that seeds future stakes without over-explaining. Dialogue is largely sharp and characterful ("You got runaway stamped on your forehead in neon pink, Tennessee"), though a few lines tip into exposition ("Mine were the kind who liked their discipline with a closed fist and a belt buckle") and Cricket's vernacular occasionally feels performed rather than lived-in. The pronoun introduction is handled a bit neatly/conveniently, and the "bruise mirrors my bathroom mirror" symmetry is a touch on-the-nose. The chapter ends on a mild, earned note of cautious trust rather than false resolution, which suits the prompt. Prose is vivid without being purple; occasional clichés ("heart hammering," "chew you up and spit you out") and some metaphor overload ("carton of milk," "biohazard," "landmines" in quick succession) mark it as very good but not masterful. Emotionally complex: fear, relief, loneliness, defiance all coexist. Minor issues: the timeline of "2:00 PM" after a morning drop-off is slightly fuzzy, and the piece leans on familiar runaway-kid tropes. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The end of the world had not arrived with a bang, nor particularly with a whimper, but rather with the sound of a server fan wheezing into permanent silence, followed by four billion people asking if anyone else’s screen had gone blank. Midas sat upon an overturned plastic laundry basket, nursing a tin mug of boiled dock-leaf tea. It tasted remarkably of warm disappointment. Opposite him, propped against a dry-rotted beanbag, sat Chewy. Chewy was an eight-inch, synthetic-furred koala bear manufactured in the dying gasps of the Early Plasticene by a company called *JoyTech Micro-Cuddles*. Time, weather, and a near-miss with a feral badger had stripped Chewy of his right ear, most of his flocked nose, and any lingering sense of moral decency. *“Bzzzt,”* Chewy’s internal speaker crackled, wet and tinny. *“Did you know? Koalas sleep twenty hours a day! Let’s learn to… G-G-GIVE UP.”* “We are not giving up,” Midas said, rubbing his temple. It was an automatic reflex. Midas’s parents had named him after the mythical king in the earnest, middle-class hope that he might show an aptitude for investment banking. Unfortunately, the universe was profoundly literal-minded, but possessed a cruel editorial streak: everything Midas touched did not turn to gold, but rather collapsed into an intricate, cascading catastrophe. If Midas picked up a pristine glass vase, physics would quietly invent a localized seismic tremor just to see the shards fly. “The writing was quite specific,” Midas insisted, pointing a soot-blackened finger toward the road. Yesterday, while fleeing an unusually aggressive swarm of bumblebees, Midas had tumbled into a dry culvert and found himself nose-to-concrete with a message scrawled in faded spray paint: *EDEN-ON-TEES. 3 MI. SW. TINNED PEACHES. HOT SHOWERS. NO ARSONISTS.* Below it was an arrow pointing toward the scrubby, unmapped wilderness that had once been an out-of-town retail park. *“Warning,”* Chewy hummed, his optical sensors—two cracked marbles of cloudy acrylic—whirring as they struggled to focus on Midas’s left collarbone. *“Low battery. Replace with two AA alkaline cells. Or… DROWN IN DITCH. Have a Koala-ty day!”* “We’ll find batteries there, too,” Midas said, hauling himself upright. “It’s three miles. A brisk constitutional. We secure the perimeter, negotiate terms of entry, and by nightfall, we are eating cling peaches from a bowl that hasn't previously held motor oil. Come on.” He scooped Chewy up and shoved him into the kangaroo-pouch pocket of his faded fleece. Chewy’s motorized paw twitched once against Midas’s ribs, like a dying cricket. *** The Great Collapse had done wonders for the local flora, which had taken one look at the sudden absence of council hedge-trimmers and declared absolute, violent sovereignty over Hampshire. The first mile was spent untangling themselves from a briar patch that seemed to possess prehensile ambitions. The second mile was complicated by the fact that the old B4011 had ceased to be a tarmac surface and had become an unpaved wetland populated by enormous, bad-tempered mallards. “You see?” Midas panted, ducking under a suspended curtain of wild clematis. His trousers were already shredded at the knee, and his left trainer had begun making a squelching sound that suggested he was treading on a small, depressed toad. “Progress. We’re definitely SW-ing.” *“Playtime is… OVER,”* Chewy announced from the pocket. *“Giggle with Chewy! Ha. Ha. Ha. Threat detected: Lateral stupidity.”* “It’s an instinct for exploration,” Midas muttered. The third mile did not reveal a shining citadel of civilization, nor did it offer the wafting scent of preserved stone fruit. Instead, it delivered them to the rusted perimeter fence of the *Oat-Crest Industrial Distribution Park*. Tied to the chain-link gate was a painted board: *EDEN-ON-TEES. KNOCK LOUDLY.* Midas beamed. “What did I say? Faith, Chewy. A little human—” He knocked. He knocked quite gently, in fact, but the gate was hung on hinges that had surrendered to oxidation during the late administration of King Charles III. With a long, operatic screech, the eight-foot iron gate sheared off its top bracket, swung inward like a pendulum, and flattened a weathered wooden lean-to directly on the other side. The lean-to, it turned out, had not been a reception desk. It had been the structural support for a carefully balanced tower of roughly three hundred empty, rusted oil drums, upon which sat a substantial colony of yellowhammers, a very irritated raccoon, and an ingenious counter-weight system designed to dump five hundredweight of river silt on intruders. *Clang.* *WHUMP.* Midas stood blinking in the newly minted crater. The air was entirely composed of pulverized rust and ancient pigeon guano. *“Wheeeee!”* Chewy chirped from somewhere near Midas’s navel. *“Press my tummy for a happy melody!”* From the darkness of the warehouse beyond came an ominous, scraping rattle. It was not the sound of welcome wagons. It sounded like several people who had spent fifteen years eating wild parsnips, and who had very rigid ideas about personal property. “Ah,” Midas whispered. “The hot showers may be a tactical fiction.” A crossbow bolt hummed through the air and took off the woolen pom-pom of Midas’s beanie. “Retreat!” Midas yelped. He spun on his good heel, caught his foot in the fallen chain-link fence, and executed a magnificent, involuntary dive into the drainage ditch he had spent the last twenty minutes skirting. *** By the time they crested the hill toward their humble gazebo at four in the afternoon, the sun was sinking behind a bruised purple cloud bank. Midas was no longer wearing his left shoe; it had been claimed by the silt-pit during their tactical withdrawal through the nettle forest. His right eyebrow was singed from what he fervently hoped had been a flare gun and not an artisanal flamethrower, and his fleece had taken on the rich, unmistakable bouquet of stagnant pond-weed. He limped into the gazebo, slumped onto the beanbag, and dropped Chewy onto the laundry basket. Chewy had not emerged unscathed. A stray pellet had punched clean through his speaker mesh, causing his voice modulator to drop three octaves into a demonic baritone. His left arm was stuck pointing straight up at the heavens in a gesture of frantic, synthetic salute, and his remaining ear was filled with pond-scum. Midas stared at the grey ceiling. A single, triumphant nettle sting was throbbing furiously on his upper lip. “Well,” Midas croaked. “We established the perimeter.” Chewy’s internal mechanism ground its gears together with the sound of a blender attempting to purée gravel. *“G-G-GOOD JOB, LITTLE BUDDY,”* Chewy growled, the demonic baritone echoing off the rotting canvas. *“TOMORROW… WE LEARN ABOUT… TAPEWORMS.”* Midas sighed, closed his eyes, and poured the dregs of the cold dock-leaf tea down his throat. “Tomorrow,” Midas agreed, “we head north.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a well-executed Pratchett pastiche: dry, wry narrator, footnote-style digressions embedded in prose, literal-minded universe jokes (the Midas naming gag), and a malfunctioning animatronic koala delivering corrupted corporate taglines as deadpan commentary. The structure faithfully follows the prompt: deliberation at home base, a mission (finding Eden-on-Tees), escalating catastrophe (gate collapse, oil drum tower, crossbow-wielding isolationists, drainage ditch), and a return home "worse for wear" in multiple senses. Strengths: Chewy's garbled "educational" programming is the comic engine and is consistently funny ("Let's learn to... G-G-GIVE UP," "Threat detected: Lateral stupidity"). The worldbuilding details are evocative and economical — the collapsed B4011 as wetland full of "bad-tempered mallards," the retail park, the spray-painted sign with "NO ARSONISTS." The slapstick set-piece of the gate shearing off its hinges into the counterweight trap is well-choreographed. The final line, "Tomorrow, we head north," lands as a perfect deadpan continuation. Weaknesses: The plot is quite thin — a sign promises paradise, paradise isn't, they flee — and the middle mile-montage is somewhat padded with comic flourishes rather than incident. Some jokes are telegraphed (the Midas "universe is literal-minded" explanation is over-explained, a mild tell). Midas himself is a sketch rather than a character: hapless everyman with no interiority beyond reflexive optimism. Emotionally the piece stays in a single comic register, so there's little complexity, though the prompt asked for wry and dry, which it delivers. The prose occasionally strains ("The air was entirely composed of pulverized rust" is a nice inversion, but a few similes feel writerly rather than found). Nothing is purple or overwrought; sentences flow cleanly. No meandering — the piece is tightly built to its ~1000-word target. Dialogue is mostly Chewy's broadcasts, which are characterful; Midas's lines are serviceable. Overall: a polished, funny, competent genre exercise that hits every instruction without transcending them. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 78.7
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the door didn’t just ring; it shrieked as the oak frame slammed shut, rattling the leaded glass. Outside, the rain was sweeping sideways down the slate-roofed high street of Aberffrwd, accompanied by the muffled shouts of three soaked men brandishing telephoto lenses like hunting rifles. Inside, Tristan Vance leaned his back hard against the wood, catching his breath. He pulled down the brim of a dripping tweed cap, adjusted the collar of his cashmere coat, and flashed his signature, thousand-watt, box-office-certified smile toward the interior. "Any port in a storm," he murmured, his voice dipping into that velvet baritone that had recently caused a minor riot at the Venice Film Festival. Behind a counter stacked with yellowed paperbacks, Carys didn’t look up from her ledger. She methodically blotted a square of blue ink with a wooden rocker. "The port is closed to loiterers," she said. Her voice had the soft, lyrical lilt of the Conwy Valley, but the tone was pure granite. "And you’re dripping on the local history section." Tristan’s smile faltered, just for a millisecond, before re-engaging with predatory charm. He took off his tinted sunglasses, shaking water droplets from them. He waited for the widening of the eyes. The gasp. The nervous fluttering of hands to hair. Nothing. She finally raised her head, looking at him with the mild annoyance one might reserve for a stray sheep in a vegetable patch. She had sharp, hazel eyes, dark curls pinned haphazardly with a pencil, and a mouth that seemed entirely immune to the gravitational pull of his presence. Inwardly, Carys’s heart was hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. *Sweet Jesus and all His saints,* she thought, her fingers tightening into a white-knuckled grip beneath the rim of the desk. It was him. *The* Tristan Vance. He was wider in the shoulders than on screen, smelled obscenely of sandalwood and petrichor, and possessed the kind of jawline that ought to require a planning permit. She resolved, instantly and with fierce Welsh stubbornness, to die before letting him know she recognized him. "My apologies," Tristan said smoothly, stepping toward the counter with an easy, fluid grace designed to disarm. "I found myself… pursued. Over-enthusiastic locals, I imagine." "They had London plates on their estate car," Carys remarked coolly, turning a page. "And an umbrella with a hole in it. Not locals. Buy something or shiver by the door." Tristan blinked. He leaned an elbow on the scarred wood of the counter, tilting his head just so—his three-quarter profile, universally agreed by cinematographers to be lethal. "You don't strike me as a woman who turns away a weary traveler in distress. Tristan." He extended a manicured hand. Carys looked at the hand. Then at his face. "Carys. And this is a business, not an abbey." She didn't take the hand. Tristan drew it back, laughing lightly, though his pride gave a sharp, indignant twinge. *Who doesn't shake my hand?* he thought, a sudden, cold panic prickling behind his ribs. Did she truly not know him? Had *The Winter King* flopped that badly in the provinces? Or worse—did she know him and find him thoroughly unimpressive? "Right. Well. Carys," he tested her name, letting it roll off his tongue with deliberate intimacy. "Perhaps a recommendation, then? To justify my shelter. What does the purveyor of fine literature suggest for a man running for his life?" "A raincoat with a hood," she said without missing a beat. Tristan let out a genuine bark of laughter. It wasn't his polished talk-show chuckle; it was rougher, caught unawares. He leaned closer, his eyes narrowing with a spark of genuine curiosity that replaced the rehearsed flirtation. "You are completely unimpressed by me, aren't you?" "I don't know you," Carys lied, smooth as butter, while the heat rose traitorously up the back of her neck. "Should I be? Did you invent penicillin?" "Worse," Tristan said, a self-deprecating smirk tugging at his mouth. "I pretend to be people who did." "Ah. An actor." She said the word as if diagnosing a mild case of dry rot. "You wound me. Deeply. Right in the vanity." He tapped his chest. But the theatrical gesture masked a sudden, unsettling truth: she *had* wounded him, just a bit. And paradoxically, he couldn't take his eyes off her. There was no artifice in her face, no clamoring for his attention, and the silence between them suddenly felt suffocatingly, thrillingly thick. "Vanity is an expensive hobby," Carys murmured, looking down to straighten a stack of bookmarks, desperate to break the magnetic pull of his blue eyes. Up close, there were faint lines of exhaustion around them. He looked fragile under the gloss, like fine china pretending to be steel. "It’s not a hobby, it’s a survival mechanism," Tristan said. The rogueish tone slipped, just a fraction. He picked up an antique brass paperweight, turning it over in his palms. "When I was twenty-two, I did a regional run of *The Seagull* in Bristol. Small theatre. Bleak winter. Second act, I completely dried. Just… nothing behind the eyes. Total, abysmal silence for what felt like forty years." Carys looked up, arrested by the change in his cadence. "The director, a miserable bastard named Halloway, cornered me in the wings after," Tristan continued, staring at the brass weight, his voice quiet. "He didn't yell. He just looked at me and said, 'The trouble with you, Vance, is that you think if you smile, we won't notice there’s nobody home.' He told me I was hollow. That the moment an audience stops clapping, I cease to exist." He set the paperweight down with a soft click and met her gaze. The mask was entirely off now, exposing the raw, hungry boy beneath the movie star. "Terrifies me," he admitted, the whisper barely carrying over the sound of rain against the glass. "Silence. Rooms where nobody looks up." Carys felt her throat tighten. The rehearsed aloofness cracked, exposing the tenderness she’d been desperately fighting. She looked at him—really looked at him—and saw the tremendous, exhausting effort it took to be brilliant every second of every day. "Halloway sounds like an idiot," she said softly. Tristan’s gaze snapped to hers, startled. "Silence in a bookshop isn't emptiness, Mr. Vance," she continued, her voice dipping lower, the Welsh cadence wrapping around the words like wool. "It’s just room to breathe. People exist here without having to perform for their supper." She reached across the counter, her fingers brushing the sleeve of his damp coat as she picked up a slender, leather-bound volume and pushed it toward him. "Dylan Thomas. Early poems. Read page forty-two." Tristan didn't look at the book. He looked at the place where her hand had touched his arm, then slowly up to her lips, and finally into her eyes. The air between them hummed like a live wire. His usual patter was gone, evaporated in the damp Welsh air, leaving behind a heavy, racing pulse he hadn't felt in years. "Will you read it to me?" he asked, his voice low, stripped of all performance. Carys swallowed, her calm veneer shattering into a quiet, breathless smile. "Ten pounds," she said, though her hand trembled slightly as she pulled it back. "Plus tax for the performance."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene executes the brief with considerable skill. The Welsh setting is established efficiently through concrete detail (slate roofs, Conwy Valley lilt, the fictional Aberffrwd), and the paparazzi premise launches the action immediately without throat-clearing. The central dynamic—Tristan's charm offensive colliding with Carys's studied indifference—is dramatized primarily through dialogue, as instructed, and both voices are distinct: his are polished, self-consciously performative lines; hers are dry, clipped deflections with Welsh texture. The character work is the piece's strongest asset. Tristan's fragile ego is rendered through small, precise beats: the millisecond falter of the smile, the "cold panic" at the unshaken hand, the internal tallying of her non-recognition. Carys's inward fluster is handled with humor ("a jawline that ought to require a planning permit") that keeps her interiority consistent with her exterior dryness. The paradox the prompt requested—that his attraction is provoked by her immunity—is genuinely present in the text, not just asserted. Weaknesses: the vulnerability reveal arrives somewhat quickly and conveniently; Tristan's Seagull confession is a well-worn device (the actor who is hollow inside), and the scene leans on it rather than finding a fresher crack in him. The Halloway anecdote is effective but borders on the confessional-cliché. There are occasional overreaches in the prose—"possessed the kind of jawline," "the air between them hummed like a live wire," "exposing the raw, hungry boy beneath the movie star"—phrases that gesture at intensity rather than earning it. Some interiority is told rather than shown ("Carys felt her throat tighten"), though the scene mostly balances this with physical action (the blotted ink, the paperweight, the book pushed across the counter). The ending is a genuine high point: "Ten pounds. Plus tax for the performance" resolves the tension with wit while conceding Carys's surrender—light, earned, and in both voices at once. The Dylan Thomas touch is apt and unforced. The scene never meanders; every exchange escalates or complicates. Overall this is polished, professional commercial romance writing with real craft in dialogue and pacing, slightly let down by a few stock images and a vulnerability beat that comes a touch too easily. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 75.9
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The iron-shod door swung inward on hinges drowned in tallow, offering neither creak nor resistance. Aya led the way into the underhold, the skin beneath her boiled-leather mask prickling with an instinct older than reason. The silence here was not the hushed reverence of a sanctuary; it was the suffocating stillness of an abattoir between shifts. The air hung cold and greasy, saturated with the unmistakable stench of refined leviathan oil—that thick, cloying musk that clung to the back of the throat like boiled fat. "Too quiet, Aya," Katra whispered, her fingers nervously picking at the brass knuckles tucked into her woolen coat. Behind them, Simeon’s heavy boots scraped the flagstones, his breathing shallow. "If the Watch took the mistress at dawn, the under-bosses should be tearing these vaults apart for the scraps." *She’s right,* Aya thought, her pulse thrumming against the delicate curve of her collarbone. *Unless there were no scraps left to fight over.* A sudden, sharp *clack* of striking flints shattered the gloom. From the iron rafters and recessed alcoves, a dozen storm-lanterns flared to life in violent unison. Green-gold phosphor light, fed by pressurized whale-grease, flooded the vaulted chamber. Aya blinked against the glare, her hand dropping instinctively to the small bone fetish sewn inside her sleeve—a conduit to the freezing, ink-black tide of the immateria that murmured beneath the crust of the mortal world. She froze. At the far end of the room, seated upon a crate of heavy harbor ordnance before the vault of the Scythan artifact, sat Madame Corva. She wore no magistrate’s chains, no signs of the black-iron holding cells at Iron-Gallows Point. She was dressed in her accustomed sea-coal velvet, a cut-throat razor resting idly between fingers scarred by harpoon line. Flanking her were six hulking dredgers, their shoulders broad as draft horses, heavy steam-compression carbines leveled with sickening precision at Aya’s chest. "Walk into my pantry, did you, little mice?" Corva’s voice was like gravel crushed beneath an iron keel. Simeon lunged forward half a step, but the cocking of six heavy brass firing pins produced a chorus of dry, definitive clicks. "Don't," Aya commanded quietly, raising her open palms. "Stand down, Simeon." To reach into the immateria now, to draw forth the pale, tooth-mouthed horrors that answered her blood, would take two seconds too long. Against steel springs and compressed steam, magick was a dying whisper. Her mother had known that too, right up until the hemp snapped taut around her throat. Two men stepped forward with practiced, brutal efficiency. One caught Simeon with a truncheon across the kidneys, dropping the big man to his knees with a choked groan; the other wrenched Katra’s arms behind her, pinning her against the slime-slick brickwork. A third man, smelling of wet dog and tobacco, seized Aya by the throat and shoved her hard against an iron support pillar. Corva approached, her heavy boots clicking rhythmically on the stone. "A raid, they said," Corva murmured, stopping inches away. "The High Bailiff’s men kicking in the wharf-doors. A clever piece of stagecraft, wasn't it? Costs fifty sovereigns to grease the Bailiff’s palms for an empty arrest, but it flushes the bilge. Shows me who among my crew has the stomach for treason." Corva drew the curved skinning blade from her belt, slid the cold flat of the steel under the edge of Aya’s leather hood, and severed the cord with a single flick. The mask fell away, clattering against the damp flags. From across the harbor, muffled by fathoms of brine and granite, a distant foghorn groaned—a long, mournful bellow that shook the marrow of the earth. *One.* Corva’s sneer faltered, her dark, coal-rimmed eyes widening as they raked over Aya’s features. There was no gutter-born grime etched into the pores of this face; no rickets in the jaw, no rot in the teeth. Here was porcelain skin, the sharp, haughty bridge of an aristocrat's nose, and eyes the distinct, crystalline violet of the old peerage. "Well, now," Corva breathed, a terrible amusement curdling her features. "What’s a darling from the upper terraces doing skulking in my sewers? You’re Lord Sterling’s get, aren't you? The little recluse who spends her allowance on dead men's books." *Stupid,* Aya berated herself, her mind spinning wildly like a carriage wheel slipped from its axle. *Stupid, arrogant girl.* She had thought herself invisible in the dark. But out here, stripped of her mask, she was not the dread shade who summoned weeping things from the ether; she was a spoiled child caught in the wolf’s den. Worse than Corva’s blade was the crushing reality of exposure. If Corva didn't kill her, her father would lock her in the asylum. Or the Ministry of Purity would sniff out the residue of the immateria clinging to her skirts, remember her mother’s blasphemies, and construct a second gallows on the green. "You can't kill me," Aya said, forcing her voice to shed its tremor, adopting the icy, dismissive cadence of the drawing rooms she so despised. "You kill me, and you sign your own death warrant, Corva." Corva tapped the blade against Aya’s cheek, drawing a single bead of scarlet. "Is that right, my lady? Down here, blood washes into the bay just the same." "A gutter rat's blood does," Aya countered, staring straight into the guild-mistress's yellowed eyes. "An heiress to the Sterling harbor-leases does not. My father doesn't care about my soul, but he cares immensely about his ledgers. If I disappear into the tide, he will pay the Ministry to burn the Lower Docks to the pilings just to find the ring from my finger." The second blast of the foghorn rolled through the stone. *Two.* Corva didn't move, but the tip of the razor eased by a fraction of an inch. "I am worth five thousand sovereigns alive," Aya pressed, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. "In non-sequential high-house scrip. Untraceable. Ten times what you'd scrape from the black market for whatever dusty Scythan trinket you have locked in that vault." "And your friends?" Corva asked, gesturing vaguely toward Katra and Simeon. "Part of the price," Aya said without hesitation, though bile rose in her throat. "They stay breathing, or you get nothing but my corpse and the full weight of the City Watch at your barricades." The third blast of the harbor horn sounded, low and ominous, vibrating through the cold grease on the walls. *Three.* Madame Corva stared at her for a long, agonizing moment. Then, slowly, she smiled—a yellow, predatory grin that promised a cage far worse than the one Aya had tried so desperately to escape. "Bind her wrists in brass," Corva commanded softly. "It seems we're moving into the ransom trade."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response delivers the requested scene competently: the trio enters the underhold, is confronted by the un-incarcerated guild leader (Madame Corva), is captured without a fight scene, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates on her value as a hostage while grappling internally with the consequences of exposure. The whalepunk/steampunk-Victorian aesthetic is well served—leviathan oil, phosphor storm-lanterns, steam-compression carbines, Iron-Gallows Point—and the "men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared" theme is woven in effectively through Aya's calculation that summoning would be too slow against spring-loaded steel. Strengths: The prose is confident and atmospheric, with strong sensory grounding (the greasy air, the tallow-drowned hinges, the foghorn motif counting one-two-three). Aya's internal monologue is present and does real work—her self-recrimination ("Stupid, arrogant girl") and her dread of the asylum and the Ministry of Purity land the gothic stakes. The dialogue is mostly differentiated: Corva's gravel-voiced menace ("Walk into my pantry, did you, little mice?") contrasts with Aya's deliberate pivot into drawing-room cadence, which is a nice character beat showing her strategic use of her aristocratic identity. Weaknesses: The foghorn counting device (One. Two. Three.) is introduced with no payoff—it reads as an ominous motif but never connects to anything, which feels like an unfinished or borrowed flourish. Corva's capitulation to the ransom argument is somewhat swift and convenient; a hardened crime matriarch weighing a razor against an heiress's throat folds a little easily, though her final predatory smile and "ransom trade" line preserve menace adequately. Some phrasing edges toward overwrought ("the freezing, ink-black tide of the immateria that murmured beneath the crust of the mortal world"), and a few clichés appear ("heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird," "grinned—a yellow, predatory grin"). Katra and Simeon are thinly sketched, existing mostly as captured bodies rather than characters, which slightly undercuts the "close companions" framing. The reveal that the arrest was staged corruption is a solid twist but is delivered in exposition rather than dramatized. Overall, this is a polished, professional genre piece that hits every requested beat with vivid atmosphere and competent characterization, falling short of excellence only in its occasional overwrought phrasing, underdeveloped secondary characters, and a couple of convenient plot turns. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 76.6
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon jukebox in the corner of the dive bar is broken, stuck in a violent, looping groove. Over and over, a scratchy guitar riff screams, stutters on a tinny drum fill, and resets, drilling the same four bars of cheap rock into the grimy floorboards. Spike Spiegel doesn’t care. He sits slumped over a scarred laminate table, a bent cigarette burning between two long fingers, watching the ash grow dangerously long. Opposite him sits an empty bowl that once held lukewarm noodles, and beside it, an ice cube melting into amber bourbon. Across the booth, Revy slams her tumbler down so hard the amber liquid sloshes over the rim. "Look, afro," she snarls, pointing a calloused finger in his face. Her Cutlass sits heavy and flat on the table, cold stainless steel catching the jukebox’s blood-red glow. "The mark is mine. I tracked that bloated cartel pig all the way from the docks. You step in front of my iron, and I’ll put a hole through that fancy blue suit." Spike exhales a lazy ribbon of smoke, tilting his head. His mismatched eyes—one real, one artificial—drift from the twin Berettas tucked into her web gear down to the tribal dragon winding up her bare shoulder, then finally to her furious, sweat-glistened face. She is wearing faded denim cutoffs and a black halter top, looking less like a professional hunter and more like a riot waiting to happen. "Sounds like a lot of running around," Spike says, his voice a low, gravelly drawl. "Waste of energy. Especially since I already tapped the guy’s comms two hours ago. He’s walking straight into the motel across the street at midnight." "You son of a bitch." Revy leans in, her dark eyes flashing with feral indignation. Her breath smells of dark rum and unfiltered tobacco. "You poached my feed?" "I wouldn't call it poaching." Spike taps his ash into an empty beer cap. "Let's call it... aggressive market research." "I'll research the inside of your skull, you cocky prick." Despite the venom, she doesn’t draw. Her gaze drops to the way his hand rests loosely near the hidden Jericho under his jacket. There is an electric stillness between them, a familiar, predatory hum. Both of them smell of burnt powder and cheap survival. For all her barking, Revy’s pupils are dilated; for all his detachment, Spike’s heart ticks just a fraction faster against his ribs. The front doors crash open before either can test the waters. Five men in armored vests burst into the bar, automatic submachine guns sweeping the dim room. The target’s vanguard, sent to sweep the perimeter. The jukebox scratches, skips, and wails its endless chord. "Guess he didn't want to wait until midnight," Spike murmurs. "Mine!" Revy roars. She moves like an uncoiled spring. Her twin Cutlasses clear the table in an arc of silver, roaring in deafening stereophonic thunder. The lead mercenary takes two hollow-points to the chest and folds backward through the swinging doors. Spike doesn’t reach for his gun immediately. Instead, he flows out of the booth, low and water-smooth, ducking beneath a stutter of 9mm rounds that chew the vinyl seats into stuffing. He plants a palm on the floor, sweeps his long leg in a wide, whistling crescent that shatters a gunman’s kneecap, and steals the man’s balance before planting an open-palm strike beneath his chin. Bone snaps. As the second man reels, Spike draws his Jericho 941 and fires two clean, spaced shots into the throat of a third. Beside him, Revy is an engine of pure fury. She steps into the line of fire without blinking, laughing with manic glee, brass casings raining around her boots like heavy hail. She empties both magazines, dropping the remaining two men in an explosion of red mist, the slides of her pistols locking back with a dual, smoking snap. Silence drops over the bar, save for the hum of neon and the jukebox, endlessly repeating its manic, four-chord loop. Revy turns to Spike, chest heaving, sweat plastering dark bangs to her forehead. She smells of cordite and copper. Spike stands casually, twirling his Jericho once before sliding it back into its shoulder holster, nursing a shallow crease where a bullet grazed his lapel. "Not bad, Two Hands," Spike says softly. "Shut up," she breathes, but her eyes rake down his lean frame, lingering on the easy, feline grace that nearly mirrors her own lethality. "The mark's across the street. And I'm not splitting the cash." *** Room 12 of the Starlight Motel smells of damp mildew and iron. The target is already dealt with—bound, gagged, and unconscious in the bathtub, bleeding quietly into the drain after Revy pistol-whipped him and Spike tied the knots. Now, the door is locked, the curtains are drawn against the flashing vacancy sign, and the room is suffocatingly small. Revy leans against the dresser, arms crossed, one hand resting on the grip of her holstered gun. Spike sits on the edge of the sagging mattress, lighting another cigarette with a worn Zippo. "He's worth eighty million woolongs," Spike says, flicking the lighter shut. "Don't give a damn about space money," Revy snaps. "In Roanapur, his head clears my tab with the Russians. You take the bounties in the sky, bird-boy. Earth belongs to me." "I'm from Mars, actually." Spike looks up through the smoke, his dark brown eye half-lidded, his fake eye steady and unreadable. "And I'm hungry. Eighty million buys a lot of beef." Revy scoffs, stepping away from the dresser. Her boots make no sound on the thin carpet. She stops two inches from where he sits, looking down at him. The heat radiating off her is palpable—a furious, raw gravity. "You talk too much." "You shoot too much." She reaches out, her rough fingers snatching the cigarette straight from his lips. She takes a long drag, exhaling the smoke right into his face, challenging him. Spike doesn't flinch. Instead, he reaches up, catching her wrist in a grip that is light, fluid, yet unyielding. Her pulse thumps wildly under his thumb. Revy’s free hand drops toward her hip, but before she can unholster, Spike pulls her downward. She tumbles onto the mattress with a sharp gasp, twisting her body to pin him beneath her, her knee driving between his thighs while the muzzle of her Cutlass presses firmly against the underside of his jaw. Simultaneously, the cold barrel of Spike's Jericho rests dead-center against the dragon on her ribs. Neither pulls the trigger. Their breathing is ragged, synced to the muffled pulse of the street outside. Her hair brushes his cheek, smelling of rain and sulfur. Up close, her mouth is soft, trembling with a volatile mixture of suspicion and desire. "I could blow your head off right now," Revy whispers, her voice dropping into a dangerous, husky register. "No more split." "You could," Spike murmurs, his gaze drifting from her dark eyes down to her parted lips, utterly indifferent to the steel under his chin. His thumb brushes the bare skin of her hip. "Or you could pull that trigger, I pull mine, and the fat guy in the tub walks out a free man." "I'm not a good person, afro," she says, her grip tightening on the grip, leaning closer until her lips are a breath away from his. "I'm just here." Spike smiles, faint and fatalistic, the ghost of an old life flickering in his mismatched eyes before surrendering to the heat of the moment. "Whatever happens," he whispers against her mouth, "happens." Their guns remain cocked between their chests as she crashes her lips against his.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers exactly what the prompt requests: a seedy bar meeting, drinking, gunplay, competitive banter, and a motel room standoff with unresolved sexual tension. Both characters are recognizably themselves—Spike's fatalism, hunger, prosthetic eye, and Jeet Kune Do fluidity are all present; Revy's foul mouth, dual Cutlasses, dragon tattoo, and volatility are well rendered. The famous quotes are woven in naturally at the climax, which is a nice touch. Strengths: The prose is confident and atmospheric. The broken jukebox motif bookends the action effectively. The action choreography is clear and kinetic without becoming muddled. The mutual gunpoint kiss is a fitting culmination of the "standoff" requirement, and the tension is genuinely charged rather than perfunctory. Character voices in dialogue are distinct—Revy's aggression, Spike's laconic deflection. Weaknesses: The bar fight arrives conveniently (the vanguard bursting in just as tension peaks is a well-worn device). Some descriptions lean on stock phrasing—"engine of pure fury," "uncoiled spring," "red mist." The worldbuilding fusion is hand-waved (woolongs vs. Roanapur money) though the story acknowledges it, which is charming rather than sloppy. Revy's vulnerability surfaces a bit quickly given her trust issues; the attraction escalates fast, though the guns-still-drawn framing preserves the "unresolved" tension. A few clichés ("smelling of rain and sulfur," "faint and fatalistic"). The ending is somewhat predictable in shape, but the execution is competent. The piece is coherent, tight, and never meanders. It shows rather than tells for the most part, with occasional slips into summarizing emotional states ("a volatile mixture of suspicion and desire"). + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Even thirty years later, whenever the frost hardens the mud along the ditch-banks, I can still taste the copper tang of Astrid’s pocketknife against my tongue. I was fifteen that October, sulking through an exile engineered by my father’s transfer to the pulp mill in Storuman. Stockholm had been concrete, neon-streaked rain, and Nirvana echoing from cassette decks in the subway; this village was nothing but spruce trees, rotting birch, and silence so vast it felt punitive. Astrid was the only girl in our year who didn't smell like damp hay or barn dust. She wore oversized army surplus jackets and silver hoops through her cartilage, and she claimed her *mormor* had been the last true cunning woman in the parish. To me, it was just better than sitting in my wood-paneled bedroom listening to the wind rattle the double-glazed windows. Astrid turned the forest into a game of dares. We stole tallow from the parish cellar, mixed lead shavings into river water to divine who Pontus from the hockey team was sleeping with, and chanted broken fragments of Latin until our scalps prickled. It was teenage boredom dressed up in old women’s superstitions. Until the night of the mound. "Útiseta," she told me behind the gym, blowing cigarette smoke through her nose like an impatient draft horse. "It means sitting out. You sit on a *gravhög* from dusk till dawn without speaking. If you don’t run, the mound-dweller tells you what’s coming." "Like what?" I asked, affecting the dry sneer I used to hide my terror. "Whether we pass the chemistry midterm?" "Like who dies before midsummer," she replied flatly. "And how to make Pontus do whatever you want." We went out past the clear-cuts, beyond where the logging roads turned to bog. The mound sat in a clearing of stunted dwarf birch—a rounded swell of earth covered in reindeer moss, like an immense belly sleeping beneath the turf. It was Iron Age, Astrid insisted, though no plaque marked it. The cold was sharp, smelling of pine needles and stagnant peat. My Doc Martens sank into the wet lichen. "Rules," Astrid said, her voice dropping into the flat, instructional cadence she used for ritual, entirely devoid of her usual mocking laugh. She produced a square of rough, coarse-spun *vadmal* wool that smelled rancid, like sheep tallow and lye. "You sit on the crest. Cross-legged. You pull the cloth over your head. You don't take it off, not even if you hear your mother calling you. If you break the boundary, bad luck follows you into the house." "Aren't you sitting with me?" "I keep the watch at the foot," she said, tapping an old iron railroad spike she carried in her pocket. "Iron at the root, bone at the top. Don't speak your baptismal name. Don't answer if it uses mine. And spit three times into your left palm if you feel your skin burn." I wanted to laugh, to make some biting remark about her grandmother’s fairy tales, but the air felt curiously thick, resistant, like wading through cold grease. I climbed the mound. The earth felt resilient beneath my boots, less like soil and more like a flexed muscle. I sat. Astrid threw the heavy, scratchy wool over my head. Darkness clamped down, thick and rank. The world narrowed to the sound of my own breath hitching against the coarse fabric and the rhythmic *crunch-crunch* of Astrid’s boots retreating down the slope. Then that ceased, too. There was only the cold. It crept up through the seat of my corduroy trousers, a deadening chill that seemed to seep straight from the mound’s core. I told myself it was just peat frost. Teenagers across Sweden were at home watching *Twin Peaks* on VHS; I was sitting under a horse blanket in a swamp because I didn't know how to tell Astrid no. Ten minutes passed. My knees throbbed. The dark beneath the blanket took on a strange, phosphorescent swirl—the optical noise of eyes straining against total deprivation. Then came the sound. Across the black expanse of the valley, through miles of dead pine and freezing fog, the iron voice of the village church bell struck once. A single, heavy toll. *Clang.* The sound rolled through the soil, vibrating against my tailbone. My stomach dropped. The parish church was four kilometers away, decommissioned for evening hours, its doors padlocked since Sunday. There was no midnight service. No sexton worked at midnight. Yet the bronze resonance hung in the freezing air, decaying with agonizing slowness, humming inside my teeth. *Midnight.* The stillness that followed was different. It possessed a weight, an active intention. A draft slipped under the edge of the blanket, smelling sharply of wet pelt and turned soil. Beside my right hip, the ground depressed slightly, as if an immense, slow-moving mass had settled onto the moss. *It’s a dog,* I thought frantically, squeezing my eyes shut beneath the wool. *A stray dog, or a badger. Astrid’s playing a trick. She crept back up.* "Astrid?" I whispered, my vocal cords dry as husk. Nothing. Then, right against the weave of the wool beside my left ear, something drew a long, rattling inhalation. It was not human. The lung capacity was too great, the breath too cold—a draft from an open cellar full of winter turnips. With that breath came a voice, or the memory of a voice, dry as birch bark rubbing in high wind. It didn't speak in Swedish, nor in words I knew, but my brain seized upon the shapes of the sounds, translating them into terrible, familiar intimacy: *Linnea. Linnea whose blood runs thin.* A weight rested against my shoulder—the heavy, unyielding lean of a sodden log. The smell was overpowering now: sweet decay, wet fur, rusted iron. *Spit three times into your left palm.* My arms were pinned by terror, locked against my ribs. The thing pressed closer. I felt the shape of fingers—or roots, or frozen wood—trace the contour of my jaw through the rough cloth, testing the flesh like someone appraising fruit in a market. *It’s just hypothermia,* my Stockholm mind screamed. *Sensory deprivation. Astrid did this to scare you.* Yet beneath the wool, the blanket began to tighten. It wasn't slack anymore; something was drawing the corners down into the earth, anchoring me to the barrow. "Astrid!" I shrieked, tearing at the wool. I ripped the blanket away, gasping, tumbling backward down the slope of the mound into the frozen scrub. The clearing was utterly empty. Astrid was standing ten paces away, pale as birch bark in the starlight, clutching the iron spike with both hands, staring not at me, but at the empty crown of the mound where the wool cloth lay. It wasn't lying flat. The cloth remained peaked and draped, holding the rigid, distinct silhouette of a seated figure, even as the wind tore through the clearing and found nothing underneath to move it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that executes the brief with considerable skill. The frame device (thirty-year recollection) is established efficiently in the opening line and remains transparent, as requested. The 1990s Swedish rural setting is convincingly textured: pulp mill in Storuman, Nirvana cassettes, Doc Martens, Twin Peaks on VHS, clear-cuts and logging roads. Astrid's ritual instructions are the highlight—matter-of-fact, specific, and mixing teenage flippancy ("who Pontus is sleeping with") with genuinely traditional detail (vadmal cloth, iron spike, baptismal names, spitting into the left palm). The ambiguity is well maintained: hypothermia and sensory deprivation are offered as explanations even as the phenomena escalate, and the final image—the cloth holding the shape of a seated figure—tips toward the supernatural without confirming it. Weaknesses are minor. The prose occasionally strains for effect ("like an impatient draft horse," "squeezing my own throat through the weave" is absent, but phrases like "the optical noise of eyes straining" and "a draft from an open cellar full of winter turnips" are evocative if slightly over-engineered). The dialogue is functional rather than rich, though Astrid's flat cadence is characterful. Some imagery is excellent ("an immense belly sleeping beneath the turf," "testing the flesh like someone appraising fruit"), while a few metaphors are stacked too densely in single paragraphs. The ending is a familiar folk-horror beat—the vacated shape—but it's executed cleanly. Character interiority for Linnea is somewhat thin beyond fear; Astrid is vivid but sketched. No meandering; pacing is tight and the word count is appropriate.
